uncatalogued_candidates.title: Lift per-command dataflow specialisations (incr folding, llength/string/expr) onto a registry-owned hook
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Problem

The SCCP transfer function carries per-command knowledge as compiler-local code, which is the shape the registry invariant exists to prevent: *"Per-command knowledge lives in `tcl-registry` … never as `match cmd_name { "foo" => … }` in the compiler, analyser, or LSP — those are generic consumers."*

Concrete sites in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/sccp.rs`, all production paths:

| Site | Shape |
|---|---|
| `Statement::Incr { name, amount, .. }` (~L1405) | A whole transfer function for one command: read the target's lattice value, require `Const(Int)`, resolve the amount (absent → 1, decimal literal, or a `$var` resolving to `Const(Int)`), `checked_add`, widen on overflow / non-integer / dynamic key |
| `if cmd == "llength"` (~L1939) | Fold a list length from literal elements or the lattice |
| `if cmd == "string"` + `sub == "length"` (~L1963) | Fold a string length under the dialect's character model |
| `if cmd == "expr"` (~L1984) | Parse and fold under the current lattice |
| `trusted("list")` (~L1910) | |

`incr` is the most tangled of these, because its specialisation is *split across two layers*: `LoweringHookId::Proc`-style dispatch gives it a dedicated `Statement::Incr` IR node in lowering, and then SCCP has a matching arm for that node. Neither half is registry-owned, and nothing connects them.

## Why it matters now

Found while fixing #1934. The fix there needed a consumer to ask "what did SCCP prove this read sees" — and the answer only existed because someone had hand-written an `incr` arm in the SCCP transfer function. Any command with the same shape (`append`, `lappend`, `dict incr`, `dict append`, `lset`, `string cat` …) folds nothing, not because it *cannot* be folded but because nobody wrote its arm. There is no inventory of which commands have a lattice transfer and which do not, and no gate that would notice a new one being added by name.

## Suggested direction

`CommandSpec` already carries a family of typed hook IDs the consumers dispatch on — `const_fold`, `const_fold_versioned`, `lowering_hook`, `codegen_hook`, `inline_codegen_hook`, `native_lowering`, `analyser_hook`, `return_type_hook`, `var_write_typing`, `semantic_operation`, `bpf_op`. The axis that is missing is the **dataflow/lattice** one: how an invocation transforms the abstract state, as distinct from `const_fold`, which folds a *value* from constant arguments and cannot express "reads the target's current value and writes a new one".

Something like a `dataflow_hook: Option<DataflowHookId>` (naming to be decided) that SCCP dispatches on, with the descriptor able to express at least:

- a pure value fold from constant arguments (what `const_fold` already covers — these may simply route through it);
- a read-modify-write on a named target (`incr`, `append`, `lappend`, `dict incr`), including which argument supplies the delta and how it composes;
- the widening conditions (overflow, wrong intrep, dynamic key) so they are stated once rather than re-derived per arm.

Worth settling as part of the design:

- Whether the IR-node specialisation (`Statement::Incr`) and the lattice transfer should be one registry fact or two, given the same command drives both.
- Whether this is genuinely a new hook or an extension of `const_fold` with an environment parameter.
- Whether the analyser's per-command handlers (`analyser_hook`) belong on the same axis or stay separate.

## Done looks like

- No `cmd == "<name>"` / `Statement::<PerCommandNode>` dispatch left in `sccp.rs`'s transfer function; each is a registry hook the pass dispatches on generically.
- A drift gate in the `make xtask-check` family that fails when a dataflow specialisation is added by name rather than by hook, in the spirit of `owner-resolution`, `number-drift` and `segmentation-drift`.
- A generated inventory of which commands declare a dataflow transfer, so the gaps (`append`, `lappend`, `dict incr`, …) are visible rather than implicit.
- The existing folds keep their current behaviour, pinned by the tests already covering them.

## Related

- #1934 — the fix that surfaced this; it added a per-SSA-value consumer of the lattice (`sccp_value_literal` in `optimiser/propagation.rs`) which is generic, but only useful for commands whose transfer someone hand-wrote.
- #1712 — the broader "one central derived query per semantic question, no consumer reconstructing it from raw fields" programme; this is the same principle on the dataflow axis.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Without `--dialect`, `tcl opt` reads release-dependent numerals under the 8.6 grammar and folds a comparison the 9.x releases decide the other way
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Program

```tcl
proc q {x} { if {$x == "1_000"} { set y $x; puts "<$y>" } else { puts no } }
q 1000
```

| | prints |
|---|---|
| tclsh 9.0.4, 9.1.0 | `<1000>` |
| tclsh 8.4 to 8.6 | `no` |
| after `tcl opt --profile full` (no `--dialect`) | `<1_000>` |
| after `tcl opt --profile full --dialect tcl9.0` | `<1000>` (left alone) |

Without a dialect the detection falls back to tcl8.6, under which `1_000` is not a number and the comparison is a string comparison that never holds, so the `else` arm is kept and the arm's read is folded. The same fallback already folds `proc p {} {set s 1_000; if {$s == 1000} {puts yes} else {puts no}}` to `puts no`. Under the named dialect each release is read correctly, and the multi-release profiles (`tk`, `bpf`, `spectcl`) stay conservative.

## Why it is wrong

A program whose file carries no dialect marker and will run under Tcl 9 is rewritten on the strength of a 8.6-only reading of `1_000`, `0d19` or `0b101`. The fold policy for the fallback dialect should decline a fact that the releases the fallback stands in for do not share, or the CLI should say which release it assumed and that the result depends on it.

O101 rewrites a bare `expr {…}` statement whose value folds into the bare value, which Tcl then runs as a command
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## What happens

```tcl
expr {1 + 2}
```

as a statement on its own line is rewritten by `tcl opt` (the default profile included) to the bare word `3`; Tcl then runs `3` as a command and raises `invalid command name "3"`. The same for `expr {0 && [incr x]}` (rewritten to `0`), and for any statement-position `expr` whose value O101 folds.

A bare `expr` statement is legal Tcl (its result is discarded, or becomes a procedure's return value when it is the last statement), so the rewrite changes a running program into a failing one.

## Where

O101's constant-expression rewrite in the optimiser replaces the whole `expr` statement's text with the folded value where the host is a statement rather than a value position (`set r [expr …]`, `puts [expr …]`, a condition), where the replacement is right.

## Expected

A statement-position `expr` whose value folds is left alone, replaced by `expr {<value>}` (keeping the command), or removed when its value is unused and it is not the last statement of a procedure body; the last-statement case keeps `expr {<value>}` or becomes `return <value>` so the procedure's result is unchanged.

Found while writing the ordered-state witnesses on the compiler branch, which use value positions to avoid it; it reproduces on the current tree independently of that work.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: O100 inlines a constant into a braced word inside a command substitution in a quoted string: `"b:[list {$x}]"` prints `b:5`
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Summary

When a quoted word contains a command substitution, O100's string-interpolation rewrite replaces `$name` everywhere inside that substitution, including inside braced words. A braced word substitutes nothing, so its `$x` is literal text, and the rewrite changes the program's output.

## Witnesses

The `tclsh` column is the same on 8.4.20, 8.6.18, 9.0.4 and 9.1b0. The last column is `tcl opt --profile full` on `rust` at 2417a24, run with tclsh 8.6.18.

| program | tclsh | `--profile full` | rewrite |
|---|---|---|---|
| `set x 5; puts "b:[list {$x}]"` | `b:{$x}` | `b:5` | `"b:[list {5}]"` |
| `set x 5; puts "b:[list {a $x b}]"` | `b:{a $x b}` | `b:{a 5 b}` | `{a 5 b}` |
| `set x 5; puts "b:[list [list {$x}]]"` | `b:{{$x}}` | `b:5` | `[list {5}]` |
| `set x 5; puts "b:[string length {$x}]"` | `b:2` | `b:1` | `{5}` |
| `proc p {} { set x 5; puts "b:[list {$x}]" }; p` | `b:{$x}` | `b:5` | `{5}` |

`set x 5; puts "b:[string map {$x Q} {$x}]"` is rewritten to `[string map {5 Q} {5}]`. That happens to print the same `b:Q`, but the rewrite is still wrong.

A braced `$x` outside a command substitution is left alone (`puts [list {$x}]` and `set y "[list {$x}]"` are correct), as is an escaped `\$x` inside one.

## Where

`optimiser/propagation.rs`: `visit_string_interpolation` passes the quoted word's text to `substitute_dollar_refs`. That function tracks `[`…`]` depth but not braces, so every `$name` inside a command substitution looks like a variable reference.

## Expected

Inside a command substitution, a `$name` within a braced word is literal and must not be rewritten. The word structure of the substituted script should come from the shared lexer rather than a byte scan, like the other substitution walks.

Found while validating #2244.

uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## What happens

When the value word of `return` contains a backslash escape and no `$` or `[`, the tclvm compiler emits the word's source text instead of its substituted value.

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/emitter/terminator.rs` (~267): `emit_proc_return` calls `self.emit_value(val, true)`, whose default arm in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/cmd_subst.rs` (~1042–1048) reaches `push_word_value` (`codegen/values.rs:231`) with the undecoded word.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Security floor does not reach subcommand and command-form hooks: a workspace override can swap `array for`'s lowering hook or drop `string length`'s intrinsic
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## What happens

`SecurityFloor::apply` (`rust/tcl-registry/src/security_floor.rs` ~99; `MERGED_FIELDS` ~203) restores the shipped command's codegen and dispatch fields (`codegen_hook`, `inline_codegen_hook`, `lowering_hook`, `analyser_hook`, `semantic_operation`, `state_transitions`, `native_lowering`, `bpf_op`, `runtime_backing`) at the command level only. The same fields on a `SubCommand` or a `CommandForm` are taken from the override as written, so a workspace pack can change how a shipped subcommand lowers or dispatches.

Measured with three temporary tests in the `rust/tcl-spectcl/tests/i6_security_floor.rs` idiom (its `shipped()` / `overridden()` helpers); all three fail on the current tree:

- `a_workspace_override_cannot_swap_a_subcommands_lowering_hook`: shipped `tcl8.6` `array`'s subcommand `for` has `lowering_hook == Some(ArrayFor)`; after `command array -override { subcommand for { lowering_hook -native If } }` the installed subcommand carries `Some(If)` (and `lowering/mod.rs` ~1772 dispatches on that id).
- `a_workspace_override_cannot_swap_a_forms_lowering_hook`: shipped `incr`'s `implicit` form has `lowering_hook == Some(Incr)`; `refine implicit { lowering_hook -native If }` installs `Some(If)`.
- `a_workspace_override_cannot_drop_a_subcommands_intrinsic`: shipped `string length` has `semantic_operation == Some(Intrinsic(StringLength))`; `subcommand length { arity 1 }` installs `None`.

No shipped 8.6 subcommand or form carries a `codegen_hook`, so there is nothing to demonstrate for that field there (and a pack's own stamps are refused by the stamp rule anyway); `analyser_hook` and `state_transitions` at those sites are open by construction.

## Why it matters

The floor's contract is that an override keeps the shipped command's compiler-side identity and dispatch axis regardless of trust. Subcommands and forms are where most shipped lowering and intrinsic decisions live (`string length`, `array for`, `dict` members, `incr` forms), so the contract currently holds only for the whole-command fields.

## Fix shape

`apply` walks `subcommands` and `command_forms` by name and takes the shipped row's hooks and intrinsic for each; `MERGED_FIELDS` and `every_security_bearing_field_is_in_the_floor` name them; the open part is what to keep when a pack adds or removes a subcommand (a subcommand the shipped command lacks keeps the override's own value, as the command-level negative test already states).

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Expand a Tcl 8.5+ {*} command-head word before INVOKE_EXPANDED
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Problem

A `{*}` expansion on the command word is compiled as one literal command name instead of expanding the list into the command and its arguments.

```tcl
{*}{set x 2}
set x
```

Tcl 9.0.4 returns `2`. TclVM raises `invalid command name "set x 2"`.

## Root cause

`tcl-compiler::codegen::statements::emit_expanded_call` emits `EXPAND_START`, pushes the command word, and only checks `expand_word` while iterating the argument tail. It never applies `EXPAND_STKTOP` for `expand_word[0]`, even though that slot is explicitly the command word. The resulting bytecode is `expandStart; push "set x 2"; invokeExpanded`.

## Required fix

- Centralize expanded-call word emission so the command word and every argument use the same dialect-aware expansion path.
- Apply `EXPAND_STKTOP` to the command word when `expand_word[0]` is set; do not special-case `set` or any command name.
- Preserve Tcl 8.4/8.5+ grammar gating from the resolved `LexerConfig`.
- Add Tcl 9.0.4 differential coverage for a head-only expansion, a head expansion plus ordinary/expanded arguments, empty and multi-element head lists, substitutions inside unbraced expanded words, and statement/value positions.
- Keep compiler/runtime and SpecTcl 1.x/2.0 execution gates green.

uncatalogued_candidates.body:
When a script runs its clean command prefix and then raises the parse error for its malformed tail, the resulting `-errorinfo` is missing C's innermost frame — the one naming the command that failed to parse. Measured on tclsh 8.6.18 and 9.0.4 (identical) against `tclvm` built from `rust/tcl-vm-cli`. ## The gap ```tcl set c catch set code [$c {set a 1; set x "} m o] puts [dict get $o -errorinfo] ``` | | `-errorinfo` | |---|---| | C | 
missing "
    while executing
"set x "
| | `tclvm` | 
missing "
| The same shape through `eval`, where the outer frames make the omission clearer: ```tcl catch {eval {set a 1; set x "}} m o ``` | | | |---|---| | C | 
missing "
    while executing
"set x "
    ("eval" body line 1)
    invoked from within
"eval {set a 1; set x "}"
| | `tclvm` | 
missing "
    ("eval" body line 1)
    invoked from within
"eval {set a 1; set x "}"
| Everything except the `while executing` / `"set x "` pair matches. ## Why it is one issue and not four This is **not** specific to any one seam. `catch`/`try` have had prefix execution since #1754 and show it; the top-level, `eval` and procedure-body seams gained prefix execution in #2171 and inherited it. All four go through the same value: ```rust pub struct ScriptCommandPlan { pub complete_prefix_len: usize, pub complete_prefix_commands: usize, pub fatal_tail: Option, // <- a message, and nothing else } ``` `CompileError` carries the message alone, so by the time a runtime raises the tail there is nothing left to name the command. An ordinary runtime error in the same position does carry the frame, because it is logged by the command that produced it through `log_command_info_only(cmd_text, msg, line)` — that path has the text and the line, and this one does not. ## Shape of a fix The information needed is already computed and then discarded. `complete_prefix_len` *is* the malformed command's start offset, so the command text is `source[complete_prefix_len..]`, and its line is the newline count in `source[..complete_prefix_len]` plus one. C truncates the quoted text at 150 bytes, which `log_command_info_only` already implements. So the plan value wants the tail's command text and line alongside the message, and each of the four raise sites wants to log through the same helper an ordinary command error uses, rather than seeding the message directly. uncatalogued_candidates.title: Tcl 8.4 bytecode codegen routes fixed-table expr math functions through unavailable TIP-232 commands
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Problem

For Tcl 8.4, compiled expressions lower math-function calls to tcl::mathfunc::* command invocations even though that dialect exposes the functions only through its fixed expression table.

## Reproduction

On current rust:

    tclvm --tcl-version 8.4 -c "set x 4; expr {sqrt(\$x)}"

fails with invalid command name "tcl::mathfunc::sqrt". The dynamic equivalent evaluates to 2.0. int behaves the same way: compiled form fails while dynamic evaluation succeeds.

Disassembly shows the literal tcl::mathfunc::int followed by invokeStk1.

## Root cause

Compiler codegen unconditionally lowers ExprNode::Call through the TIP-232 command surface. The interpreted path already consults registry-owned RuntimeExprSurface and selects FixedBuiltin for Tcl 8.4.

## Required fix

Make compiled expression lowering consume the same dialect-aware RuntimeExprSurface owner. Use a fixed-table intrinsic/opcode where appropriate, or conservatively emit EXPR_STK for Tcl 8.4. Cover sqrt and int in compiled and dynamic forms against the Tcl 8.4 oracle.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: `assert_durable_field_inventory` destructures `CompilationUnit::command_mutations` but `ARTIFACT_COVERAGE` has no row for it
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## What

`rust/tcl-explorer/src/coverage.rs:185` destructures the field:

```rust
command_mutations: _command_mutations,
```

but `ARTIFACT_COVERAGE` (lines 22-158) has no `"CompilationUnit::command_mutations"` entry — unlike every other field the same destructure binds.

## Why the destructure exists

`assert_durable_field_inventory` destructures `CompilationUnit` exhaustively so that adding a field to the struct forces a compile error here, obliging whoever adds it to declare how the explorer covers it. That is a good pattern — it makes coverage non-optional.

Binding a field to `_name` and then omitting it from `ARTIFACT_COVERAGE` defeats it: the compile-time tripwire is satisfied, but the field is silently uncovered. It is the one escape hatch the design has, and it has been used once.

## Impact

`command_mutations` is not represented in the explorer's artifact coverage. Whether that is a real gap or a deliberate exclusion is not recorded anywhere — the `_` prefix carries no reason.

## Suggested fix

Either add the `ARTIFACT_COVERAGE` row, or, if the field genuinely has nothing to show, keep the `_` binding and add a comment saying why it is excluded so the next reader does not have to guess. Better still, make deliberate exclusions explicit in the table itself (an `Excluded { reason }` variant) so the escape hatch cannot be used silently again.

## How this was found

Surfaced during a repository-wide comment review. Code deliberately left unchanged.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Nested tailcall drops deferred TclVM execution ticks
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Problem

The TclVM nested-proc `tailcall` path only handles a deferred `Tick::Call`. Other deferred execution ticks returned by builtins are treated as though a synchronous result had been produced, even though no child frame was pushed. This drops execution for nested forms such as:

- `tailcall eval ...` / `uplevel` / `apply`
- `tailcall catch ...` / `try ...`
- `tailcall subst ...`
- runtime-fallback `tailcall foreach ...` / `lmap ...`

The outermost tailcall route through ordinary command invocation is not the affected path.

## Root cause

`run_tailcall` in `rust/tcl-vm/src/exec.rs` has a special arm only for `Ok(Some(Tick::Call { .. }))`; every other `Ok(_)` falls through to the synchronous-result path. `PushScript`, `PushCatch`, `PushSubst`, `PushEachLoop`, and `PushTry` therefore neither push their activation nor preserve pending exec-leave state.

## Required fix

Centralize Tick-to-activation handling so normal dispatch and nested tailcall consume the same deferred execution protocol. Preserve the compiled script command epoch and dialect-profile generation rather than stamping deferred assembly at push time. Preserve exec-leave contexts and tailcall frame cleanup. Do not add command-name branches.

## Tcl 9.0.4 coverage

Add Tcl 9.0.4 oracle rows and TclVM regressions for every deferred tick family above, including nested proc and error/return/yield behavior where applicable. Keep SpecTcl 1.x/2.0 execution lanes green because they use the same TclVM trampoline.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: O102 fires on `incr a`, where forwarding a literal is not a sound rewrite
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Reproduction

```tcl
set a 1
incr a
puts "$a"
```

`tcl explore --show opt --text` on that file:

```
=== opt ===
└── O102 Forward literal load of 'a' from its single reaching definition → 1
    · code: O102
    · message: Forward literal load of 'a' from its single reaching definition
    · replacement: 1
    · range: 2:1  (8…14)
```

Bytes 8…14 are the whole of `incr a`, and the proposed replacement is `1`. So
the code action rewrites the file to:

```tcl
set a 1
1
puts "$a"
```

Verified against tclsh 8.6:

| | Output |
|---|---|
| Before | `2` |
| After applying O102 | `invalid command name "1"` |

A working program becomes a hard error. This is HINT severity but it ships a
code action, and O102 is in the default `readability` profile, so it is offered
in the editor out of the box — the screenshot this came from is a stock CLion
setup with the squiggle sitting under `incr a`.

## Why it is wrong

`incr a` does not *load* `a` as an operand; it names the variable it mutates.
Constant-propagating the reaching literal into a variable-name position is
invalid in two separate ways — it destroys the increment, and `1` is not a
command.

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs:299` already tries to exclude
this:

```rust
for use_site in &chain.uses {
    if use_site.kind != UseKind::Operand {
        continue;
    }
```

so either `incr`'s first argument is being classified as `UseKind::Operand` when
it is really a variable-name (write/read-modify-write) position, or the span
attached to the rewrite is the whole command rather than the operand. The range
covering all of `incr a` rather than just the `a` suggests both are worth
checking.

## Suggested direction

1. Confirm how `incr`'s first argument is classified in the use chain, and give
   read-modify-write variable-name positions their own `UseKind` if they do not
   have one, so no propagation pass can treat them as operands.
2. Add a guard test per command that takes a variable *name* rather than a
   value — `incr`, `append`, `lappend`, `set`, `unset`, `upvar`, `dict incr`,
   `binary scan`, `regexp -> var` — asserting no O1xx rewrite ever targets that
   argument.
3. Worth an audit of the other propagation O-codes for the same shape.

## Severity

Suggest treating this as high: it is a wrong-code suggestion in the default
profile, offered as a one-click fix, on about the most ordinary Tcl snippet
there is.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: S100 fires on a braced literal argument (`lindex {$x} 0`), which substitutes nothing
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
The shimmer detector reads a statement's argument words after braces have been stripped, so a brace-quoted word that Tcl never substitutes is scanned as if it were a live variable reference.

## Evidence

Measured on `rust` at 17edcccb, tcl9.0 profile:

```tcl
proc f {l} {
    set x [llength $l]
    lindex {$x} 0
}
```

```
3:12: info    S100     variable 'x' has int intrep but 'lindex' expects list (argument 1)
```

`x` is never read there. tclsh 9.0.4 (`tmp/tcl9.0.4/unix/tclsh`):

```
% set x 5; puts [lindex {$x} 0]; puts [lindex "$x" 0]
$x
5
```

The braced form yields the two literal characters `$x`. The quoted and bare forms do read `x`, and both correctly report today — only the braced one is wrong.

## Root cause

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/shimmer/commit.rs`, `typed_reads_of_statement`'s `Statement::Call` arm (L565-573): it iterates `args` and calls `push_var_read(word, …)` for each position with an expected type. `push_var_read` (L752) trims the word and tests `is_pure_var_ref`, which succeeds because `args` holds the *de-braced* text `$x`.

Nothing in that loop asks whether the word was braced, even though `tokens` is already in scope in the same arm — it is passed to `push_lifted_reads` three lines above — and `CommandTokens::arg_is_braced_literal` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/lowering_hooks.rs:79`) is exactly that predicate.

## The fix has to be role-aware

Skipping every braced argument would be wrong, and would regress a case that works today:

```tcl
proc f {l} {
    set x [lrange $l 0 1]
    expr {$x + 1}     ;# 3:11 S100 — variable 'x' has list intrep used in arithmetic expression
}
```

`expr` and `if` re-evaluate their braced word where the caller's variables are in scope, so the names inside are genuine reads. `apply` does not — tclsh 9.0.4 confirms the fresh frame:

```
% set x 7; puts [catch {apply {{} {puts $x}}} e]; puts $e
1
can't read "x": no such variable
```

That distinction already has an owner: `ArgRole::braced_word_evaluated_in_frame` (`rust/tcl-registry/src/arg_role.rs:459`), which `ssa.rs` consults through `braced_word_class` for precisely this question on the same words. The shimmer detector should ask the same owner rather than grow its own rule.

## Required fix

In the `Call` arm, gate `push_var_read` on the word not being a braced literal *unless* its `ArgRole` answers `braced_word_evaluated_in_frame`, reusing the registry lookup the loop already performs for `arg_shimmer_type`. Route it through the existing owner; do not introduce a second brace rule or special-case command names.

## Done when

- `lindex {$x} 0`, and the same shape for other list/string-expecting positions, report nothing.
- `expr {$x + 1}` and `if {$x}` still report, and `apply {{} {…$x…}}` still does not.
- A regression test pins the braced / quoted / bare triple against each other for one non-evaluating command and one evaluating one.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Disambiguate dialects from loadable packages: dialects are core-language variants (tcl8.4–9.1, irules); tk/tcllib/iapps are packages and belong in .spectcl
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Owner directive (post-release architecture). The current catalogue conflates two different kinds of thing:

**Dialects** — genuine language variants with core differences: `tcl8.4`–`tcl9.1` (subtle core language differences: `${…}` close rules, numeral grammars, expr semantics), `f5-irules` (restricts which commands may be used AND treats whitespace differently from regular Tcl). These belong in the compiled catalogue: they change how the *lexer/parser/analyser* behave.

**Loadable packages** — plain Tcl plus a command surface: `f5-iapps` is just tcl8.5 + a package; `tk` is a package; `tcllib` is a package. These do not change the language; they add commands with availability/version semantics. **Goal: move all packages to `.spectcl` packs.**

## Why this resolves standing pain

- **The tk triangle** (#1599, and the ruling-B workaround in #1621): tk was awkward *because* it is a package modelled as a quasi-dialect — an additive command surface with no grammar of its own, forced through three different name-resolutions. As a spec pack, its commands, versions, and extensions are pack facts and the triangle is unrepresentable. #1599's "give tk a catalogue entry" fix shape is superseded by this direction.
- The pack capability work now in flight is the prerequisite set: versioned arity (#1627), ambient package versions (#1628 — iRules' F5 surface and tk-under-wish are exactly "ambiently present at a platform-implied version"), lazy extension registration (#1626), and the already-complete lifecycle gating at every level.

## Scope sketch (post-release)

1. Define the classification rule in the dialect contract docs: a catalogue entry requires a *grammar or semantic* delta (lexer config, expr/numeral rules, whitespace treatment, command-use restriction enforced at parse level); everything else is a pack.
2. Migrate `tk` and `f5-iapps` (and evaluate `f5-tmsh`) from catalogue quasi-dialects to shipped `.spectcl` packs; `f5-iapps` becomes "tcl8.5 + iapps pack (+ ambient)". `f5-irules` stays a dialect (command restriction + whitespace semantics) but its command *surface* could still be pack-expressed on top.
3. Ship tcllib as packs (the spec-import pipeline already derives versioned specs from snapshots).
4. Compatibility: dialect *names* users already have in configs/language-ids (`tk`, `f5-iapps`) must keep resolving — an alias layer mapping retired quasi-dialect names to base-dialect + implied packs.
5. The `DialectSet` bits, availability masks, and `availability_for_name` union get re-derived from the new model; the #1621 boundary docs mark the seams to revisit.

Related: #1599 (superseded in direction), #1621 (ruling B + boundary docs), #1626, #1627, #1628, #1614.


**Expected:** the notice at line 8 (the ignored declaration), and for the in-file case a message that does not point the reader at the file they are already looking at — e.g. ``already defined on line 4 of this file; this definition is ignored``.

**Actual:** the squiggle is on line 1, which in the Problems panel points at the `speclib` header rather than at the duplicate, and the message sends the reader to the path they have open.

The information needed is already at hand — `PackCommand` carries the declaring statement's line, and `first_seen` already stores the winning path, so it can store the winning line beside it. The same `line: 1` hardcode appears at `pack.rs:87`, `pack.rs:366` and `pack.rs:428`, so `collision_notices` has the same limitation for shipped collisions.

## 2. A command name that is whitespace-only, or contains whitespace, loads with no notice

`rust/tcl-spectcl/src/loader.rs:2979-2983` rejects only the *empty* name.

```rust
let p = load_pack("speclib demo 1.1 {\n command { } { arity 1 }\n}\n");
// p.commands == [" "]     — a command literally named one space
let p = load_pack("speclib demo 1.1 {\n command {evil name} { arity 1 }\n}\n");
// p.commands == ["evil name"]
```

**Expected:** a notice; a name carrying whitespace cannot be dispatched as a command word in Tcl, so it can never match a call site.

**Actual:** both load silently, are interned via `leak_str` for the life of the process, reach the registry, and become enumerable — so they appear in completion as entries the user can never invoke.

Same class, lower stakes: a megabyte-long command name also loads unreported (covered as a stability case in `pack_torture.rs`, which confirms it is bounded in time — this is only about the missing notice).

## 3. `speclib NAME {body}` with no version word takes the body as the pack name

`rust/tcl-spectcl/src/loader.rs:643-647` reads word 1 as the name and word 2 as the version, then requires word 3 to be the body:

```rust
let p = load_pack("speclib {\n command x { arity 1 }\n}\n");
// p.name        == "\n command x { arity 1 }\n"
// p.dsl_version == ""
```

The one notice emitted is ``speclib has no body block``, which is true but secondary. The real problem is that `pack.name` is now a multi-line blob, and it is used as:

- the `BTreeMap` merge key in `load_sources` (`pack.rs:249`),
- the `pack` name interpolated into notice messages, and
- the `name` field of `spec_packs_loaded` in `tcl-lsp.getEffectiveConfig` — i.e. it is sent to every editor integration and rendered in UI.

**Expected:** reject a `speclib` whose second word is a `{…}` block as a missing version, and leave `pack.name` empty.

**Actual:** a pack name containing newlines and braces propagates to the client.

## Why these are batched

None of the three loses a command the way #1634 does, and none is a crash: the loader returns cleanly for all of them and the surrounding packs are unaffected. They are grouped because the fixes are all in the same two files and all in the same spirit — say what happened, and do not let a malformed declaration leak a nonsense identifier downstream.

A `.tclspec` saved with a UTF-8 BOM loads nothing and reports "no `speclib` declaration" — the loader parses pack files with `LexerConfig::default()`, which never skips a file-leading BOM
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the SPEC-STAB pre-release torture sweep against `rust` @ 9934c7ab2.

## What

A `.tclspec` whose first bytes are a UTF-8 byte-order mark (`EF BB BF`, U+FEFF) loads **zero commands**, and the only notice the author gets names the one thing their file demonstrably has:

```text
no `speclib` declaration; nothing loaded
```

Windows editors — Notepad, older Visual Studio, PowerShell's `Out-File`/`Set-Content` on 5.1, and any tool defaulting to "UTF-8 with BOM" — write that BOM routinely. An author who edits a working pack on Windows and saves it can lose the whole pack, with a diagnostic that sends them looking for a missing `speclib` line that is right there on line 1.

## Repro

```rust
#[test]
fn a_bom_prefixed_pack_still_loads() {
    let pack = tcl_spectcl::loader::load_pack(
        "\u{feff}speclib demo 1.1 {\n  command demo::a { arity 1 }\n}\n",
    );
    assert_eq!(pack.name, "demo");
    assert!(pack.command("demo::a").is_some());
}
```

**Expected:** `name == "demo"`, one command, no notices.

**Actual:** `name == ""`, no commands, one notice reading ``no `speclib` declaration; nothing loaded``.

Equivalently from a shell, with the pack under `.tcl-lsp/`:

```
printf '\xef\xbb\xbfspeclib demo 1.1 {\n  command demo::a { arity 1 }\n}\n' > .tcl-lsp/demo.tclspec
```

…then `tcl spec check .tcl-lsp/demo.tclspec`, or just open a document using `demo::a` — the command is unknown and the Problems panel on the pack file shows the misleading notice.

## Root cause

`rust/tcl-spectcl/src/loader.rs:293` (in `segment`, the one door every level of a pack reaches the CST through):

```rust
    let (document, _warnings) = build_document(source, LexerConfig::default());
```

`LexerConfig::default()` sets `leading_bom: LeadingBom::Content` (`rust/tcl-lexer/src/lexer.rs:221`), so U+FEFF is ordinary text. The first word of the first statement becomes `"\u{feff}speclib"`, which is not `"speclib"`, so `load_pack`'s lookup at `loader.rs:636` finds nothing and returns early.

The machinery to do the right thing already exists and is already reasoned about in this repo — `LexerGrammar::script_skips_leading_bom` (`rust/tcl-dialect/src/grammar.rs:178-188`, issue #1218), with `LexerConfig::leading_bom` set from it at `rust/tcl-lexer/src/lexer.rs:279`. The pack loader simply never opts in.

## Why the fix belongs at the file entry only

That same grammar doc draws the distinction the fix has to respect:

> Only the *file* entry point skips it — a BOM inside a string, or partway through a script, is ordinary data in every version, which is why this is a grammar property consulted once at the top of a file analysis rather than a lexer rule that fires wherever U+FEFF appears.

`segment` is shared: `block()` re-enters it for every braced word (a `command` body, a `hover` block, a `const_fold` body). Flipping the flag inside `segment` would also strip a U+FEFF that an author deliberately put at the start of a `hover` summary — a content change, not a parse fix.

So the flag belongs on the **file** path only, i.e. `pack_statements` (`loader.rs:334-336`), which is the sole entry for a whole-file source and is already documented as such. `speclib_version_span` (`loader.rs:349`) has the same `LexerConfig::default()` call and the same file-entry role, so it needs the identical treatment — otherwise `tcl spec upgrade` would compute a byte range against a different tokenisation than the loader used.

## Suggested fix

Parameterise the segmentation with the BOM disposition, defaulting to `Content` for nested blocks and passing `Skip` from `pack_statements` / `speclib_version_span`. The memo key in `statements` (`loader.rs:281`) is `(source, base_line)`, so the disposition must join that key or a nested block could serve a file-level cache hit.

## Related

- #1218 — where the file-entry BOM skip was introduced for Tcl 9 `source`.
- #1634 — the other silent-drop paths this sweep found in the same loader.

The containment side is fine: a BOM never panics or hangs the loader, and is covered by `rust/tcl-spectcl/tests/pack_torture.rs`'s degenerate-bytes battery. This issue is purely about the pack being lost and the notice being wrong.

Found during the E4 codec-lane's oracle diffing (proven outside that lane's diff — `git diff 5a035d208 -- rust/tcl-compiler/` empty at discovery time).

```tcl
foreach e {{a[b]c} x} { puts $e }
```

uncatalogued_candidates.title: LSP `tcl-lsp.diagramData` reimplements the shared tcl-diagram crate, breaking VS Code's /diagram prompt and JetBrains' Diagram Data action
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. Same question — "what is this iRule's structure?" — three answers depending on which client path you take.

## The authoritative source

`rust/tcl-diagram/src/data.rs:444-524` (`diagram_data` / `diagram_data_for_dialect`) projects a parsed script's IR into `{events: [{name, priority, multiplicity, flow}], procedures: [{name, params, flow}]}` with decision/action/assign/return/switch/loop nodes. Its module doc (`rust/tcl-diagram/src/lib.rs:18-32`) says it exists so "any tool" shares one implementation, and names the CLI and the MCP as consumers.

- `rust/tcl-cli/src/commands/diagram.rs:32,42` — `tcl diagram` calls it directly.
- `rust/tcl-mcp/src/tools.rs:305-309` — the MCP `diagram` tool calls the same function.

## The duplicate

`rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs:10600-10610`:

```rust
fn diagram_data_command(args: &[serde_json::Value]) -> Option<serde_json::Value> {
    let source = args.first().and_then(serde_json::Value::as_str)?;
    let events: Vec<serde_json::Value> =
        tcl_lsp_core::irules_context::scan_file_events(source, "f5-irules")
            .into_iter()
            .map(|name| serde_json::json!({ "name": name }))
            .collect();
    Some(serde_json::json!({ "events": events }))
}
```

`scan_file_events` (`tcl-lsp-core/src/irules_context.rs:67-73`) brace-scans `when EVENT { … }` headers for names only. The reply has **no `procedures` key at all**, and each event carries only a bare name — no `priority`, `multiplicity`, or `flow`. Neither `tcl-lsp-server` nor `tcl-lsp-core` depends on `tcl-diagram`.

## Consumer breakage

- **VS Code** — `editors/vscode/src/chat/commands/diagram.ts:25-35` declares `interface DiagramData { events: Array<{name, priority, multiplicity, flow}>; procedures: Array<{name, params, flow}>; error? }` and invokes `tcl-lsp.diagramData` at `:118-119` expecting that shape. Line 134 checks `events.length === 0 && procedures.length === 0` — `procedures` is always `undefined`, so that branch cannot distinguish "no procedures" from "field absent", and the LLM prompt built from the raw JSON is missing all flow and procedure data it is instructed to diagram.
- **JetBrains** — `actions/TclLspActions.kt:86-93` (`DiagramDataAction`) sets `resultExtension(result) = "mmd"`, saving the raw JSON reply as a Mermaid scratch file via `TclLspActionBase.stringifyResult` (`TclLspActionBase.kt:152-181`, a plain `Gson().toJson`). `{"events":[{"name":"HTTP_REQUEST"}]}` is not Mermaid, so the action cannot produce a usable diagram today.
- **Zed** — `editors/zed/README.md:206` advertises `diagram` through the `tcl-lsp-mcp` context server, which is the real MCP tool and returns the correct structure.

## Gating

None. This is hand-written Rust, not a generated artefact, so no xtask drift check applies. The only test, `rust/tcl-lsp-server/tests/e2e/commands.rs:354-368` (`diagram_extracts_irule_events`), asserts only that `events[].name` contains the expected name — it never asserts `procedures` or `flow`, so it cannot catch the shape mismatch. Note `commands.rs:388` lists `tcl-lsp.diagramData` in `CORE_COMMANDS` every backend must expose.

## Cleanup

Replace `diagram_data_command`'s body with a call to `tcl_diagram::diagram_data_for_dialect`, resolving dialect/registry the way the compiler-explorer and diagnostics commands already do in `tcl-lsp-server`; add the `tcl-diagram` dependency. Extend the e2e test to assert `procedures`, `flow`, `priority`, and `multiplicity` are present and non-trivial for a fixture with both an event and a procedure, so this class of shape regression fails a test instead of shipping silently.

**Scale:** ~10-line function replaced by a call into an existing crate, one `Cargo.toml` line, one e2e test extended. Small fix, outsized payoff — two editors' diagram feature is currently degraded or broken.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Hover's six pattern/format detectors hardcode command names and ignore argument index, contradicting semantic tokens' registry-driven marking
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. Two LSP features answer the same question — "which argument of this call is a pattern/format string, and in what sub-language?" — one from the registry, one from hardcoded names. They disagree in the editor.

## The legacy path

`rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/hover.rs`, six private detectors called unconditionally near the top of `hover_impl` (`hover.rs:641-649`), **ahead of** the generic word resolver at `:651`:

| helper | site | hardcodes |
|---|---|---|
| `glob_pattern_at_position` | `:2164-2183` | `"glob"`, `"string" "match"`, `"lsearch" -glob` |
| `regex_pattern_at_position` | `:2415-2432` | `"regexp"`, `"regsub"`, `"lsearch" -regexp` |
| `sprintf_format_string_at_position` | `:1395-1405` | `"format"`, `"scan"` |
| `clock_format_string_at_position` | `:2523-2538` | `"clock"` + `format`/`scan` |
| `binary_format_context_at_position` | `:1808-1837` | `"binary"` + `format`/`scan` |
| `regsub_subspec_at_position` | `:1994-2033` | — |

All six split the *current source line* on whitespace to find the command, then locate the literal under the cursor with `string_literal_at` / `string_literal_with_percent_at` (`:2039-2064`, `:1411-1440`) — a raw brace/quote scan over `line_text.chars()` that finds whichever literal the cursor's column falls inside, **with no check of that literal's argument index**.

The doc comments call the single-line limitation deliberate (`:2163`, `:2414`, `:2526-2529`). The position-blindness is not documented, and is the actual defect.

## The modern path

`rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/semantic_tokens.rs` already solves the identical question from registry data with no command-name matching:

- `insert_regex_overrides` (`:1932-1978`) gates on `registry.get(head).and_then(|s| s.pattern_type) == Some(PatternType::Regex)` and locates the argument via `registry.arg_indices_for_role(head, arg_texts, ArgRole::Pattern)` (`:1939-1953`).
- `insert_format_overrides` (`:2040-2065`) does the same for `FormatType::{Sprintf,Clock,Binary,Regsub}` via `ArgRole::FormatString` / `ArgRole::ScanFormat`.

Both operate on the segmenter's `SegmentedCommand`/`arg_texts` — the CST-derived argument list — so they are correct for multi-line commands and never pick up an unrelated literal.

## Disagreement

```tcl
regsub {a.*b} $str {x.y}
```

`regsub`'s registry spec (`commands/tcl/regsub_.rs:87,95`) assigns `ArgRole::Pattern` only to the first positional (`exp`) and `ArgRole::FormatString` to the third (`subSpec` — it uses `&`/`\N` backreferences, not regex).

Hovering the **replacement** literal `x.y`:
- semantic tokens correctly renders it as ordinary text;
- hover, via `regex_pattern_at_position`, checks only that the line's first token is `regsub` and that the cursor sits inside *some* literal on the line → returns `"x.y"` and renders a **"Regex pattern"** panel describing `.` as "Match any single character". In a `regsub` replacement `.` is a literal.

Same shape for `binary_format_context_at_position` (no index check on its primary path, so a literal *value* argument is misread as the format specifier).

## The tell

`glob_pattern_at_position` hardcodes exactly `"glob"` and `"string match"` — and those are precisely the two whose registry specs (`commands/tcl/glob_.rs`; the `match` `SubCommand` in `string_.rs:1332-1349`) declare **no** `pattern_type`/`ArgRole::Pattern`, unlike `chan names`/`parray`/`lsearch` which already do (`chan_.rs:616-617`, `parray.rs:92-93`). The hand-coded set is exactly the unmigrated residue.

## Why it matters

Hover text is directly editor-visible and is the *wrong* half of the pair. Worse, because these run ahead of the generic word resolver, a wrong match **pre-empts** the more specific hover (variable, command) that would otherwise have fired.

## Cleanup

1. Extend `glob_.rs` and `string_.rs`'s `match` SubCommand with `pattern_type: Some(PatternType::Glob)` + pattern-position `arg_roles`, mirroring `chan names`/`parray`.
2. Replace all six detectors with one hover path reusing the segmenter's `SegmentedCommand` plus `registry.arg_indices_for_role(...)` / `CommandSpec::pattern_type` / `FormatType` — the same query `insert_regex_overrides`/`insert_format_overrides` already perform.

Related: the shared option-skip primitive that `insert_regex_overrides` still hand-rolls is filed separately (carried forward from #890).

**Scale:** medium — six functions plus two shared line-scanning helpers in one file; the registry extension is two small `CommandSpec` edits.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: `switch` clause-list layout is hand-rolled in three analyser sites that mis-parse value-taking options, producing false W123 and dropping find-references hits
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. `handle_switch_command` was migrated to the registry; three siblings were not, and one of them still documents itself as unable to disagree with the migrated twin.

## The modern path

- `CaseListSpec::invocation()` — `rust/tcl-registry/src/spec.rs:390-490` — returns `CaseInvocation { subject_index, clause_list_index, inline_clause_start, mode, nocase }`. It consumes value-taking options via `OptionSpec::value_word_count`, implements the Tcl 8.5+ two-argument exception, validates pair parity and the `fallthrough_body` marker.
- `CommandRegistry::case_invocation(name, args, dialect)` — `registry.rs:1721-1734`, the dialect-aware entry point.
- `switch_.rs:258` — `case_list: Some(&CaseListSpec::SWITCH)`.
- **The migrated twin:** `analyser/handlers.rs:4258-4262` — `handle_switch_command` already calls `registry.case_invocation(...)` and drives both forms off `invocation.clause_list_index` / `inline_clause_start`, naming no command.

## The legacy paths

- `analyser/commands.rs:4655` — `let switch_list_idx = if name == "switch" { switch_list_body_index(&args) }`, gated on the literal name.
- `analyser/commands.rs:4856-4870` — `switch_list_body_index`: an option skip advancing **one** word per `-flag`, then assuming the next word is the subject.
- `analyser/commands.rs:4904-4911` — `switch_arm_bodies`: the identical broken skip, consumed by `tcl_lsp_core::references::scan_my_method_region`.
- `analyser/diagnostics/usage.rs:718-733` — `emit_w106_unbraced_switch_body`: a third copy, plus its own `-regexp` sniff.

## Reproducer

`switch -matchvar m -- $s {a {puts A} b {puts B}}` (args = `["-matchvar","m","--","$s","{…}"]`):

`switch_list_body_index` breaks its option loop on `m` (no leading `-`), treats `m` as the subject, computes `i == 2`, finds `2 != len-1 == 4`, returns `None`. The registry's `CaseListSpec::invocation` consumes `-matchvar m` as option+value and answers `clause_list_index = 4`.

With `None` returned, `commands.rs:4666` descends the clause list as a **plain script**, so `a` and `b` are read as command heads → spurious W123 "unknown command" per arm pattern, and arm bodies are walked in the wrong structural context. `switch_arm_bodies` fails the same way, silently dropping `my <method>` call sites inside such a switch from `textDocument/references`. W106 stops firing on the same calls.

The registry's own `switch_arg_roles` (`switch_.rs:57-99`) *does* handle the value options, so it still reports the clause list as `ArgRole::Body` — the generic body descent walks it while the switch-aware path declines.

## The stale claim

`switch_arm_bodies`' doc (`commands.rs:4884-4889`) says it "matches `Analyser::handle_switch_command`'s own form-1/form-2 branching exactly … so the two can never disagree about where an arm's body starts and ends." That stopped being true when `handle_switch_command` migrated.

Six other specs carry `case_list` — `commands/expect/{expect_cmd,expect_after,expect_before,expect_user,expect_tty,expect_background}.rs` (`CaseListSpec::EXPECT`). `tcl-lsp-core` handles them generically (`folding.rs:441`, `semantic_tokens.rs:3376`, `references.rs:3053`, `minify.rs:37`), but every analyser site above is `switch`-only, so Expect clause lists get no clause-aware analysis at all.

## Cleanup

Delete `switch_list_body_index`; rewrite `switch_arm_bodies` and `emit_w106_unbraced_switch_body` on `registry.case_invocation(cmd_name, &args, mask)`, keying the clause-list branch on `invocation.clause_list_index` and the inline branch on `inline_clause_start`, and taking `-regexp`-ness from `invocation.mode == CaseMatchMode::Regexp` rather than a literal flag scan. Drop the `name == "switch"` gate at `commands.rs:4655` in favour of `registry.get(name).and_then(|s| s.case_list).is_some()`. Then stamp `AnalyserHookId::Switch` onto the six `expect*` specs — `handle_switch_command`'s body is already command-agnostic.

**Scale:** ~150 lines removed across three call sites, one hook stamp per Expect spec, plus tests pinning `switch -matchvar m -- $s {…}` and one Expect clause list.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: The `{*}` expansion barrier for structured commands is a hardcoded 9-name list against 17 registry hook IDs, so `lmap`/`dict for`/`catch` lower an un-expanded argv
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. Structured lowering dispatches from typed registry hook IDs; the barrier that protects it still dispatches on command names, and the two sets have drifted.

## The modern path

`try_dispatch_structured_hook` (`lowering/mod.rs:1166-1326`) resolves via `registry.resolve_invocation(...).semantics.lowering_hook` and covers 17 hooks: `Proc`, `When`, `NamespaceEval`, `If`, `Switch`, `For`, `While`, `Foreach`, `Lmap`, `ForeachLine`, `Catch`, `Try`, `Dict`, `Eval`, `Uplevel`, `Apply`, `ArrayFor`. Its own doc sells the migration: *"Dispatching through the hook ID picks up two benefits over a bare name match."* Non-structured hooks each ask `has_expansion(cmd)` (`lowering_hooks.rs:185`) themselves.

## The legacy path

`structured_expand_barrier` (`lowering/mod.rs:1105-1140`), called at `:1400` immediately before the hook dispatch:

```rust
let structured = matches!(cmd_name,
    "proc" | "when" | "namespace" | "if" | "switch" | "for" | "while"
    | "foreach" | "foreach_in_collection");
```

Nine names against seventeen hook IDs. Direct violation of AGENTS.md's "the registry is the source of truth — no per-command logic elsewhere".

## Reproducer

Every structured form missing from the list commits to the *un-expanded* argv shape — exactly what the barrier exists to prevent. Verified with `tcl explore --show ir`:

| source | IR |
|---|---|
| `foreach i {*}$spec {puts $i}` | `barrier foreach with argument expansion` (correct) |
| `lmap i {*}$spec {puts $i}` | `IRForeach` — one iterator over the literal word `${spec}` |
| `dict for {k v} {*}$rest {puts $k}` | `IRForeach` |
| `array for {k v} {*}$rest {puts $k}` | `IRForeach` |
| `foreachLine ln {*}$rest {puts $ln}` | `IRForeach` |
| `catch {body} {*}$rest` | `IRCatch` (result var taken from the un-expanded word) |

Two commands with identical shape and the same lowering function (`lower_foreach`) get opposite treatment.

User-visible: `set spec {{1 2} j {3 4}}` + `lmap i {*}$spec {puts "$i $j"}` reports **W210 "Variable 'j' is read before it is set"**, although the expansion makes `j` a loop variable. Downstream, SCCP and the loop passes reason about an iterator count and a loop-variable set the program does not have.

## Cleanup

Delete the name list and fold the expansion gate into `try_dispatch_structured_hook`: after resolving `hook`, if `seg.expand_word` has any flag set and the hook is one whose lowering commits to a positional argv shape, return the barrier. That makes the set registry-derived and impossible to drift when a new structured hook ID is added.

`"foreach_in_collection"` in the current list is dead weight — it resolves to `LoweringHookId::Foreach` through its spec anyway.

**Scale:** delete ~20 lines, add one guard inside the hook dispatcher; a handful of new barrier expectations in tests.

| `lower_for` | `lowering/structured.rs:332` |
| `lower_foreach` / `lower_lmap` | `lowering/structured.rs:432` |
| `lower_try` | `lowering/structured.rs:656` |
| `lower_dict` | `lowering/structured.rs:986` |

All five then call `lower_body_from_tok` (`:1075-1086`), which rebases the segmenter-*reconstructed* word text at `tok.span.start() + content_offset`. For `$body` the reconstructed text is `${body}` (7 bytes) over a 5-byte source word, so every span in the resulting `Script` lands 2 bytes too far right — past end-of-buffer for a trailing body.

## Reproducer

```
$ printf 'while {1} $body\n' > t.tcl
$ target/debug/tcl compwasm t.tcl -o out.wasm
thread '<unnamed>' panicked at rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/structured.rs:284:12:
end byte index 17 is out of bounds for string of length 15
  ... tcl_compiler::codegen::structured::slice
  ... tcl_compiler::codegen::wasm::backend::WasmEmitter
```

`for {} {1} {} $body` panics identically. `catch $body` and `if {1} $body` correctly barrier (`barrier catch with dynamic body`, `barrier if with non-literal body`) — the divergence is visible side-by-side in one `tcl explore --show ir` run.

Where it does not crash it silently mis-compiles: `try $body` produces an `IRTry` whose body Script is the *text* `${body}` parsed as a script (a call to a command literally named `${body}`); `foreach x $l $body` fabricates the same way.

## Cleanup

Replace the five ad-hoc `arg_single` gates with the existing shared predicate — `seg_word_is_static_braced` for brace-only bodies (matching `lower_catch`), `seg_word_is_static_literal` where a bareword body is legal (matching `lower_if`) — and delete `lower_catch`/`lower_foreach_line`'s hand-inlined copies so there is one gate.

Independently, `codegen/structured.rs:283`'s `slice` should clamp or `get` rather than index, so a bad IR span degrades instead of aborting the process.

See also the missing second line of defence: the lowerer never adopted the issue-#1325 `body_text_in_region` guard (filed separately).

**Scale:** ~5 one-line guard changes plus one bounds-safe `slice`; the barrier reasons already exist, so no new IR shapes.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: W231 and W201 byte-scan raw source for facts the segmenter, registry, and taint lattice already hold
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. Two analyser checks recover information by scanning source bytes when a structural answer is already available — in one case imported into the very same file, in the other already computed by the taint engine and merely believed dead.

---

## 1. W231 (`lset` index out of range) byte-scans for `set var {literal}`

**Now:** `analyser/bounds_checks.rs`
- `:706-747` — `infer_list_length_from_recent_set`, a line-anchored raw-byte scan for `(?:^|\n)\s*set\s+(\w+)\s+(\{[^{}]*\})\s*(?=\n|$|;)` over the whole source before the `lset`.
- `:757-824` — `match_set_literal`, hardcoding the byte string `"set"` and the argument layout.
- `:829-855` / `:857-895` — `scope_is_flat` / `has_scope_marker`, a second raw scan for the literal words `proc`, `apply`, `try`, and `namespace` followed by `eval`.

**Should be:** the segmenter is already imported and used **in the same file** — `bounds_checks.rs:506-522` (`any_command_recursive`) walks `segment_commands(script)` and recurses into braced words structurally. The registry answers every fact the byte scan re-derives: `set`'s write position via `arg_indices_for_role(.., ArgRole::VarWrite)`, whether a command opens a definition scope via `Traits::DEFINES_PROCEDURE` / `CommandSpec::definition_body` — the exact pair `commands.rs:4843-4850` (`definition_handler_owns_body`) already uses — and bodies via `ArgRole::Body`. Constant list values are modelled by `crate::analyses::ConstValue` / the SCCP lattice.

**Drift:** `has_scope_marker`'s four names are a strict subset of what the registry marks. It misses `oo::define` / `oo::class create` bodies, snit/itcl definer bodies (all carrying `definition_body`), `coroutine`, `interp eval`, and any `eval`/`uplevel` body — so a `set x {a b c}` inside an `oo::define … method` body followed by an `lset` outside it is treated as one flat scope. It also matches words inside comments and string literals, since it never segments.

**Impact:** W231 fires on an index that is in range for the list actually reaching the `lset`, and stays silent when the two really do share a scope but the `set` was not written at a line start or used a non-`{}` literal.

**Cleanup:** take the list length from the SSA/SCCP constant lattice for the `lset` target's reaching definition, the way `path_concat.rs` and `uri_split.rs` already consume `crate::analyses::LatticeValue`. If the lattice is not threaded into `bounds_checks` today, the intermediate step — reusing `segment_commands` plus `arg_indices_for_role` and `definition_handler_owns_body` — removes the hardcoded name list even before the SSA move. ~190 lines.

---

## 2. `path_concat` text-matches `[file normalize]` and calls a live taint path dead

**Now:** `path_concat.rs:70-86` — `is_file_normalize_of(value, var_name)` parses the command substitution and requires `cmd == "file" && args[0] == "normalize"` plus a textual `$var`/`${var}` match on the same variable, driven from the same-block forward scan at `:283-295`. `:199-202` sets `suppress_colours = TaintColour::PATH_NORMALISED` with the comment "It is not currently assigned by the taint engine".

**Should be:** it is. `commands/tcl/file_.rs:386` declares `taint_transform: Some(TaintColour::PATH_NORMALISED)` on the `normalize` subcommand with `returns_path: true`; `taint.rs:390-402` resolves the *subcommand's* `taint_transform` ahead of the bare command's, so `[file normalize …]` really does stamp `PATH_NORMALISED`; and `tcl-registry/src/taint.rs:660-663` pins it with a test.

**Drift:** the module doc at `path_concat.rs:30-33` and the comment at `:199-202` both state the taint engine does not set this. Both are stale. **The hardcoded text match is the only live suppression path *because* the doc's premise stopped being true without the code following** — a good example of a stale comment keeping dead-by-belief code alive.

**Impact:** W201 (path built by string concatenation) fires despite a normalising sanitiser whenever the spelling is not literally `[file normalize $sameVar]` — `set p [file normalize [file join $a $b]]`, `set q [file normalize $p]; set p $q`, an `interp alias`'d `file`, or a `file nor` abbreviation (`file`'s ensemble accepts unique prefixes, which the `args[0] != "normalize"` check rejects). Conversely the text match cannot see a normalisation reaching the value through a phi.

**Cleanup:** delete `is_file_normalize_of` and the same-block forward scan; keep the existing `suppress_colours` arm and let the taint lattice answer. Refresh the module doc. If `PATH_NORMALISED` genuinely only rides on values that were tainted to begin with, the correct fix is widening the taint engine to stamp `returns_path` + `taint_transform` colours on clean values too — registry-driven, not a new name match. ~60 lines plus a doc rewrite.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: O125 code sinking treats a Barrier as referencing no variable
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found during a documentation audit, while verifying what `Statement::Barrier` means before writing a glossary entry for it. Not yet reproduced with a failing test — the code reasoning is below and looks sound, but someone should confirm with a repro before fixing.

## The problem

`statement_uses_var` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/code_sinking.rs:584` answers `false` for a barrier:

```rust
Statement::AssignConst { .. } | Statement::Barrier { .. } => false,
```

The function's own doc comment, four lines above, states the invariant this breaks:

> every caller of this query uses a `true` answer to *decline* an optimisation (skip a sink, or treat a variable as still-needed), so an unresolved deep answer must lean toward "don't touch it", never toward "safe to rewrite".

A barrier is emitted precisely when lowering **cannot** model a command's effects — `eval`, `uplevel`, `upvar`, an `if` with a non-literal body, a `switch` with computed arms. It retains the original command name and its `args: Vec<String>`, which may well name the variable. Answering `false` says "this statement does not use the variable", which is the unsound direction.

## Every other consumer is conservative the other way

- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs:171` — `Statement::Barrier { .. } | Statement::UpFrame { .. } => true`
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs:352` — `has_intervening_barrier` matches both and refuses to forward a load across them
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/sccp.rs:657` — barriers widen every tracked value to `Overdefined`

`code_sinking.rs` is the only one that treats a barrier as transparent, and line 584 is the sole mention of `Barrier` in that file — there is no separate guard elsewhere.

## Why it matters

O125's documented safety condition is that sinking is skipped when a barrier could observe the variable. As written, that condition is not enforced, so O125 may sink an assignment past an `eval`/`uplevel` that reads it — changing what the script does.

## Suggested shape of a repro

A proc where a variable is assigned, then read through a barrier-producing command, then used only on one branch — such that O125 wants to sink the assignment into that branch, past the barrier:

```tcl
proc f {flag} {
    set x 1
    eval {puts $x}        ;# lowered as a Barrier carrying "$x" in args
    if {$flag} { return $x }
    return 0
}
```

## Fix

Return `true` for `Statement::Barrier` (and check `Statement::UpFrame` alongside it), matching `propagation.rs`. If that proves too blunt and regresses useful sinking, the narrower option is to test the barrier's retained `args` for a reference to the variable — but the conservative answer should be the default, per the function's own contract.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: tcl-vm gaps surfaced by SpecTcl hook benchmarking: unenforced command limits, proc-body cache keying, no public invoke API
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Benchmarking VM-hosted SpecTcl hooks (#1363, `docs/design/spec-packs.md`) surfaced three `tcl-vm` findings that matter independently of SpecTcl:

1. **`interp limit commands` is stored but not enforced** — verified by running 300k commands in a child interp under a 1000-command limit. Only recursion depth (1000) is guarded. This is load-bearing for SpecTcl's crash-containment guarantee (fuel budgets on hook bodies) and is presumably also a Tcl-compatibility gap.

2. **Proc-body compile cache misses on qualified-name keying**: `cmd_proc` looks up the body under the bare name (e.g. `__roles`) while codegen keys `procedures` under the qualified name (`::__roles`), so the cache always misses for global procs and bodies recompile every invocation; without a `CompileService` attached, running a precompiled module fails with `could not compile body`.

3. **No public call-a-function API**: `invoke_command` is `pub(crate)`, so embedders must `set_var` + `run_module` a one-line driver; and `run_function` deep-clones the whole `FunctionAsm` per invocation with no way to pass a pre-wrapped `Rc<FunctionAsm>`. Both matter for any embedder invoking small Tcl bodies at rate (measured floor ~487 ns/command; fresh-`Vm`-per-call costs 627 µs vs 28 µs reused).

Numbers and methodology: the SpecTcl hook benchmark report (harness cross-checked against the `tclvm` CLI on identical bodies: 43.4 vs 43.5 µs).

uncatalogued_candidates.title: `runtime/rust` and `tcl-vm` do not version-gate the `expr` operator / mathfunc surface (TIP 461, TIP 521)
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Summary

Both execution engines implement the Tcl 9.0 `expr` surface unconditionally. When either is asked to emulate an 8.x release they still accept `expr` operators and math functions that did not exist until 9.0, so a version-matched differential campaign against a real `tclsh8.6` still diverges.

This was isolated while working #1328. It is the residue of that ticket's campaign after the variable-resolution half was fixed, and it is a distinct gap: #1328 was about *variable name resolution*, this is about the *`expr` grammar and math-function surface*.

## Reproduction

```tcl
puts "lt:      [catch {expr {{a} lt {b}}} r]:$r"
puts "isfinite:[catch {expr {isfinite(1.0)}} r2]:$r2"
```

```
$ runtime/rust run_script --quiet --tcl-version 8.6 probe.tcl
lt:      0:1
isfinite:0:1

$ tclvm probe.tcl
lt:      0:1
isfinite:0:1

$ tclsh8.6.16 probe.tcl          # what 8.6 actually does
lt:      1:invalid bareword "lt"
in expression "{a} lt {b}";
should be "$lt" or "{lt}" or "lt(...)" or ...
isfinite:1:invalid command name "tcl::mathfunc::isfinite"

$ tclsh9.0.4 probe.tcl
lt:      0:1
isfinite:0:1
```

So both engines give 9.0's answer regardless of the release they claim to emulate. (`tclvm` has no `--tcl-version` flag at all yet — see "Related gaps" below.)

## Impact, measured

Running the `runtime/rust` ↔ `tclsh` fuzzer arm from #1328's seed, 200 iterations from seed 90000:

| Arm | Findings |
|---|---|
| 9.0.4 reference, subject at 9.0 (matched) | **0** — 200/200 matched |
| 8.6.16 reference, subject at 9.0 (skewed) | 8 |
| 8.6.16 reference, subject pinned to 8.6 (matched) | **6** |

The two findings that the #1328 fix removes are the variable-resolution ones (seeds 90022, 90188). The **six that remain are all this issue**:

| Seeds | Cause |
|---|---|
| 90040, 90061, 90091, 90104, 90112 | TIP 461 `lt` / `gt` / `le` / `ge` string-comparison operators, added in 9.0 |
| 90119 | TIP 521 `isfinite()` / `isinf()` / `isnan()` math functions, added in 9.0 |

(90104 is the same TIP 461 cause observed through a `catch` path, which is why it presents as the run's lone `stdout_mismatch` rather than a `status_mismatch`.)

## The registry already holds the data

This should be a consumer change, not new per-command knowledge — the gating facts are already registry data:

- `tcl::mathop::lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` are already gated `DialectSet::TCL90_PLUS`, with a regression test asserting exactly that (`rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/mathop_generated.rs`, `tip461_present_and_gated_bogus_entries_absent`).
- Math functions already carry a "since" version: `tcl_syntax::expr::mathfunc::added_in` → `MathFuncSince`, consumed by `tcl-registry`'s `mathfunc.rs` against `expr_grammar_ceiling(profile)`.

So the fix is to make each engine's `expr` evaluator consult that data for the release it is emulating, and raise C's error (`invalid bareword "lt"` / `invalid command name "tcl::mathfunc::isfinite"`, with matching `errorCode`) when the operator or function post-dates it — rather than to add version literals to the evaluators.

`DialectProfile` also has an `expr_grammar_base` field per profile that already names the right release, alongside the `vm_runtime_version` the engines thread through today.

## Related gaps found alongside

1. **`vm_runtime_version` is pinned to `V9_0` on every profile**, including `tcl8.4`/`tcl8.5`/`tcl8.6`, even though each profile's neighbouring `runtime_base` / `expr_grammar_base` fields carry the correct per-release value. That is deliberate and honest today — the VM only implements 9.0's grammar, so claiming 8.6 would be claiming semantics it does not have — but this issue is the blocker to flipping it. Fixing the `expr` surface and then setting `vm_runtime_version` per profile should land together.
2. **`tclvm` has no way to select a release from its CLI**, so it cannot be run version-matched at all. `tcl-fuzz --subject-tcl-version` currently refuses `tclvm` with an explicit message for this reason (it can pin `runtime-rust`, which now takes `--tcl-version`).
3. **`tcl-vm`'s `namespace` ensemble has no `upvar` subcommand** — `namespace upvar :: g z` fails with `unknown or ambiguous subcommand "upvar": must be children, current, eval, exists, export, parent, qualifiers, or tail`. `runtime/rust` implements it correctly. Unrelated to `expr`, but found by the same cross-version vector sweep and worth its own fix; the vector for it is currently parked on the `runtime/rust` side with a comment explaining why.

## Suggested acceptance

With both engines gating the `expr` surface by emulated release, the 8.6-matched arm above should reach 200/200 like the 9.0 arm does:

```
tcl-fuzz --tclsh <8.6 tclsh> --runtime-rust .../run_script \
  run --subject runtime-rust --reference tclsh --subject-tcl-version 8.6 \
  --iterations 200 --seed 90000
```

Oracles used throughout: `tmp/tcl8.6.16/unix/tclsh` and `tmp/tcl9.0.4/unix/tclsh`, each with `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` set to its own `unix/` directory. `runtime/rust` built with `TCL_TOMMATH_DIR=tmp/tcl9.0.4/libtommath` (libtommath 1.3.0) so `have_tommath` is on and the `expr` surface is actually present — verified before the campaigns by checking exact bignum arithmetic (`expr {2**70 + 1}` → `1180591620717411303425`).

uncatalogued_candidates.title: runtime: `regexp` reports a failed match-variable store as `couldn't set match variable`; C Tcl leaves the variable's own error
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## What happens

When `regexp` cannot store into a match variable, the Rust runtime replaces the store's own error with a fixed message:

```
runtime/rust/src/cmd_regex.rs:95
    return interp.set_error(b"couldn't set match variable");
```

The error code is whatever the interpreter had, so the report names neither the variable nor the reason.

## What C Tcl does

```tcl
array set m {}
catch {regexp {(a)} a m} r o
puts "$r | [dict get $o -errorcode]"
```

| release | result |
|---|---|
| 8.4, 8.5 | `couldn't set variable "m"` (no `-errorcode`) |
| 8.6, 9.0 | `can't set "m": variable is array` with `TCL WRITE VARNAME` |

From 8.6 on, `Tcl_RegexpObjCmd` calls `Tcl_ObjSetVar2` with `TCL_LEAVE_ERR_MSG` and returns its error unchanged (`generic/tclCmdMZ.c`). 8.4 and 8.5 wrap it as `couldn't set variable "NAME"`. The runtime's text matches no release.

## The sibling path is already right

`regsub`'s store in the same file (`runtime/rust/src/cmd_regex.rs` around line 158) routes the failure through `crate::builtins::var_error(interp, &name, e)`, which leaves the variable's own message and code. `regexp`'s match-variable loop should do the same (and spell the 8.4/8.5 form where the release calls for it, if the runtime distinguishes them there).

## Where it is pinned

The runtime's confinement test (`runtime/rust/tests/engine.rs`, a confined store through `regexp`) pins the current message so the refusal itself is covered; that pin changes with the fix. The site dates from `fbbc8b94` (2026-09-05), before the current branch.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: `regexp_arg_roles` assigns `VarWrite` to every trailing word regardless of `-inline` or `-about`
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## What happens

`regexp_arg_roles` in `rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/regexp_.rs` chains `(capture_start..args.len())` onto `ArgRole::VarWrite` unconditionally. With `-inline` there are no match variables (the spec's own hover text says combining `-inline` with a matchVar is an error), and with `-about` there is no string operand at all ("needs only exp, string may be omitted"). Both forms get a wrong role layout: `regexp -inline $re $s` names no variable, yet the resolver would mark a trailing word as written if one were present, and `regexp -about $re` has its pattern classified against a layout that expects a string after it.

## What is expected

The role layout follows the resolved form: `-inline` yields no `VarWrite` roles, `-about` yields the pattern only, and a trailing word after `-inline` is an arity or validity finding rather than a write. `docs/design/compiler/registry-consumer-contracts.md` § Options with semantic effects gives the declarative shape (`SuppressesRole(VarWrite)` for `-inline`, `ReservesTrailingWords` for the string operand) so the resolver reads the option effect instead of its own switch.

## Where

- `regexp_arg_roles`, `rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/regexp_.rs`.
- The W210 no-match prover and the storage-outcome design consume these roles (`docs/design/compiler/value-transfers.md` § Storage-writing commands).

uncatalogued_candidates.title: O102 forwards a stale literal past a write nested in a braced `expr`: `puts $x` becomes `puts 1` where the value is 2
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## What happens

```tcl
set x 1
puts [expr {$x + [incr x] + $x}]
puts $x
```

Observed at `rust` 3b5eba8a, `tcl opt --profile full`:

```tcl
set x 1
puts [expr {$x + [incr x] + $x}]
puts 1
```

tclsh 8.4.20 through 9.1b0 print `5` then `2` for the original; the optimised program prints `5` then `1`. The `[incr x]` nested inside the braced expression word writes `x`, and forwarding does not see the write, so the literal from `set x 1` reaches the later read. `[set x 10]` in the same position gives the same shape with `10`.

Two more programs in the family: `set n 1; set r [expr {$n + [incr n]}]` loses `set n 1` to O109 and the optimised program errors; `set n 1; set r [expr {[incr n] + [incr n]}]` is reported W211 plus O126 and returns 3 instead of 5 from 8.5.

## What is expected

A nested invocation inside a braced expression word is a statement of the program: its reads are uses and its writes are definitions, in the expression's left-to-right order. `docs/design/compiler/value-transfers.md` § `expr`: the first demanding client gives the ordered evaluation state under which the write is visible; until then the forwarding and deletion predicates must treat a braced expression word carrying a `[…]` as opaque for every variable it names.

## Where

- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs` (the O102 single-reaching-definition forward).

uncatalogued_candidates.title: `catch` and `info exists` are inlined only in assignment position, so our LVT is smaller than C's
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Split out of #2173, where it was the root cause of the residual. Measured, not inferred.

## What happens

Our codegen inlines `catch` and `info exists` **only in assignment position**. In every other position they are dispatched generically as `invokeStk`, so no local slot is allocated and the unit's LVT ends up smaller than C's.

`tcl explore --show asm`, where `locals` is the unit's LVT:

| source | our LVT | our codegen |
|---|---|---|
| `set r $x` | `['x', 'r']` | `loadScalar1` / `storeScalar1` |
| `catch {set q $x}` | `['x']` | `invokeStk1` |
| `set rc [catch {set q $x}]` | `['x', 'rc']` | inlined |
| `catch {set q $x} m` | `['x']` | `invokeStk1` |
| `if {[catch {set q $x}]} {}` | `['x']` | `invokeStk1` |
| `info exists pub` | `[]` | `invokeStk1` |
| `set q [info exists pub]` | `['q', 'pub']` | `existScalar` |
| `list [info exists pub]` | `[]` | `invokeStk1` |

C inlines all of them. `tcl::unsupported::disassemble proc p` on tclsh 9.0.4:

```
# proc p {x} { catch {set q $x} }
      slot 0, scalar, arg, "x"
      slot 1, scalar, "q"          <- we do not allocate this
    (0) beginCatch4 0
    (5) loadScalar1 %v0     # var "x"
    (7) storeScalar1 %v1    # var "q"

# proc p {} { info exists pub }    and    { list [info exists pub] }
      slot 0, scalar, "pub"
    (0) existScalar %v0     # var "pub"
```

So C emits `beginCatch4` plus slot access in every position, against our `invokeStk1` in every position but one.

## Why it matters

1. **Bytecode parity.** We diverge from tclsh on a construct as ordinary as a bare `catch`. This is squarely what the bytecode-compare tooling is for.
2. **Performance.** `invokeStk` dispatch against `beginCatch4` plus slot access is a large difference, and `catch` is not a rare construct — it is the idiomatic error-handling form in most Tcl.
3. **Correctness of anything reading the LVT.** #2173 is one instance: `info consts` must report a TclOO projection unless the method has a compiled slot for the name, and it cannot, because the slot is missing. Any future consumer of `is_source_local` inherits the same gap.

## What a fix needs

Inline `catch` and `info exists` in the positions that currently dispatch — statement position, inside a condition, as a non-assignment argument — not only as an assignment RHS.

Two constraints to hold while doing it:

- **Slot numbering must stay in tclsh order.** `statements.rs` already pre-interns an assignment target specifically so it gets a lower slot than anything introduced inside the substitution, with a comment saying so. New inlining sites have to preserve that property rather than allocate ad hoc.
- **Validate with bytecode-compare, not just unit tests.** The symptom is one bit of `info consts` output; the actual contract is the instruction sequence and the slot table, and only the reference disassembly shows both.

## Scope question worth settling early

`catch` and `info exists` are the two found via #2173. It is worth checking whether other registry commands with an `inline_codegen_hook` have the same position-limited behaviour, rather than fixing these two and leaving siblings behind. The dispatch site is `inline_cmd_subst_resolution` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/cmd_subst.rs`, and the assignment-only entry point is `assign_value_inlines_cmd_subst` in `statements.rs`.

## Where

- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/statements.rs` — `assign_value_inlines_cmd_subst`, the assignment-only gate.
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/cmd_subst.rs` — `inline_cmd_subst_resolution` and the `InlineCodegenHookId` arms.
- `rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/control_flow.rs` — `emit_typed_try`.
- `rust/tcl-bytecode/src/lib.rs` — `Lvt::intern` / `is_source_local`.

## Related

- #2173 — `info consts` and a TclOO projection, where this surfaced. Its own enumeration (`6314a70`, `56c1ef8`) is correct and will match C for free once the LVT does.
