uncatalogued_candidates.title: wasm codegen: the legacy analysis tier registers a proc's written body text, not the value its statement produced
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found while fixing the equivalent defect in the native tier (#1774 / #1895). Filing it separately rather than folding a silent second fix into a PR about the native tier.

## The defect

`try_emit_direct_operation` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/codegen/wasm/backend.rs` emits

```
tcl_codegen_proc_register(name, params_raw, body_source)
```

using `Procedure.body_source` — the **written** word — even where the statement's word-evaluation instructions produced a different value. For a definition whose body word is a substitution, the two differ:

```tcl
proc make {} { set body {return hello} ; proc p {x} $body }
```

records `body_source: Some("${body}")` while the compiled body came from `return hello`.

Two consequences if the path is ever reached: `info body p` reports the substitution word instead of the body, and any fallback to source — a step trace, or a declined native entry — evaluates that substitution **in the procedure's own frame**, where the variables it names may not exist.

## Why it is latent today

It cannot produce a wrong answer through any tier at present, because two unrelated conditions must coincide and currently cannot:

- both materialising paths (`const_map_lookup`, `eval_subst_nocommands_body`) bail out at `proc_depth == 0`, so materialisation only happens **inside** a procedure body;
- no procedure-body site is ever proven — those units lower under `DispatchEntryAssumption::UnknownWorld`, so `analyse_dispatch_stability` returns the empty analysis.

A top-level `proc $name {x} [subst -nocommands {return $default}]` registers no `Procedure` at all: `check_proc_body_dynamic` barriers it. The analysis and default tiers both answer `hello` / `return hello`, matching the 8.6.16 and 9.0.4 oracles.

That is a coincidence between two independent proofs, not a design — which is exactly why it is worth closing before something else changes.

## Fix shape

The same guard the native tier now uses (`88769a5`): a definition's name, parameters and body must each be written out literally, and the recorded parameter and body text must be the word's own; anything else keeps the generic invocation, where the runtime's `proc` evaluates the word at the call site as Tcl does.

Because the live path is unreachable, a sample would be a vacuous test. The native-tier fix instead removes the coincidence in the test — lowering the enclosing body under `PristineRegistryWorld` so the site *is* proven — and asserts the definition falls back to `GenericInvoke`. A sibling test shows a written-out body still binds under that same proof, so the rule is about substitution rather than a blanket refusal. The same technique applies here.

## Why it matters later

P5 plans to make procedure bodies proven. At that point both conditions hold simultaneously and this becomes live: a wrong `info body`, and a source fallback evaluating a substitution in the wrong frame.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: tclvm aborts the whole script on a later parse error where C evaluates earlier commands first (per-command parse model)
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Pre-existing, found by the #1568 adversary. `puts A` followed by `puts "x${abc"` → tclsh 8.6.16/9.0.4 print `A` and *then* raise `missing close-brace for variable name`; tclvm prints nothing and raises up front. General to `missing "`, `missing close-bracket`, etc.

C's model: each command is parsed (all of its words) immediately before evaluation — so earlier commands run, and within one command no word evaluates until the whole command parses (`puts "[side]pre${abc"` never runs `side`; oracle-confirmed). The VM's whole-script up-front parse aborts everything.

This is a script-level evaluation-model divergence rather than a single-command bug; observable by any script with trailing malformed text after meaningful work.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Harden the lowerer as a span producer: adopt the #1325 body-rebase guard and drop the dialect-blind second tokeniser
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. Two front-end helpers exist in a correct form and a hand-rolled form; in both cases the lowerer — the *producer* of the spans and facts everything downstream trusts — kept the hand-rolled one.

---

## 1. The issue-#1325 body-rebase guard was adopted by the analyser only

**The guard:** `segmenter::contiguous_prefix` (`segmenter.rs:376-394`) and `segmenter::body_text_in_region` (`:411-421`) exist specifically because rebasing a body word's spans by `tok.span.start() + content_offset` is only truthful while the word's *value* is a verbatim slice of the source. Their doc names the real incident: a compound `{body}x` word slid every token one byte left, and 40 zero-width spaces in a real iRule produced an offset inside a UTF-8 sequence that panicked the first consumer to slice the source (#1325).

**Adopted by:** the analyser's `analyse_body` (`analyser/commands.rs:220-239`) — and nothing else. `body_text_in_region` / `contiguous_prefix` have exactly one production caller in the workspace; everything else is `tests/span_char_boundaries.rs`.

**Not adopted by:** `Lowerer::lower_body_from_tok` (`lowering/structured.rs:1075-1086`), which performs the same rebase with no guard:

```rust
let offset = tok.span.start() + u32::from(tok.content_offset);
self.lower_body(text, offset, namespace)
```

and `lower_body_inner` (`lowering/mod.rs:945-952`), which feeds that straight to `segment_commands_with_offset_and_config`.

**Why it matters:** this is the missing second line of defence behind #1375. With the guard in place, `while {1} $body`'s 7-byte `${body}` against a 5-byte source region would be clamped instead of producing spans past end-of-source, and the WASM emitter would not abort. More generally, IR spans are the contract every downstream consumer trusts (AGENTS.md: *"Trust it rather than re-deriving"*) — and today the analyser side of the pipeline produces trustworthy ones while the lowering side does not.

**Cleanup:** give `Lowerer` the document source (it already receives it in `lower`/`lower_into_script` but does not retain it) and route `lower_body_from_tok` through `body_text_in_region(source, base, tok.span.end(), text)` the way `analyser::commands` does. Add a `debug_assert` in `Script::from_statements` (or `lower_segmented`) that no emitted span exceeds the document length, so a future producer cannot regress this silently. One field, one call site, one assertion; the helper is already written and tested.

---

## 2. `ir_helpers::tokenise_command_words` is a second, dialect-blind tokenisation loop

**The single splitter:** `segment_commands_with_offset_and_config` (`segmenter.rs:328-341`), CST-backed since the migration (`:807-823`) and **dialect-aware** — it threads `LexerConfig::for_dialect`, which controls `{*}` expansion (off for Tcl 8.4 and iRules) and the iRules `}{` ghost separator. Every body re-segmentation in the lowerer threads `self.config` for exactly this reason (`lowering/mod.rs:918`, `:946`; the field at `:760` and its doc spell out the contract). `SegmentedCommand` already exposes `texts`, `argv` kinds, `single_token_word`, and `expand_word`.

**The duplicate:** `ir_helpers::tokenise_command_words` (`ir_helpers.rs:587-630`) re-implements the loop by hand — `Lexer::new(source)` with `LexerConfig::default()`, its own `prev_is_sep` accumulator, its own word-concatenation rule, and its own `CommandWord { text, raw, substituted, braced_literal }` record whose doc (`:571-577`) concedes that `raw` reads back as `{s` for a braced word.

Its one caller is `dynamic_names::scan_script_text` (`dynamic_names.rs:542`), which feeds `scan_command` and therefore `DynamicNameBarrier` — consumed by SCCP (`sccp.rs:1061`) and stored on the CFG (`cfg.rs:240`) and compilation unit (`compilation_unit.rs:630`).

**Why it matters:** the barrier is an *optimisation-soundness* fact ("does anything here write through a computed variable name?"). Deriving it from a differently-configured tokenisation than the one that built the IR means the two disagree on word boundaries for any non-default dialect: under `f5-irules` the segmenter splits `cmd {a}{b}` into three words and this loop into two; under `tcl8.4` the segmenter treats `{*}` as a literal word and this loop as an expansion marker. A word-boundary disagreement changes which argument index `scan_command` inspects, so a dynamic write can fail to raise the barrier and SCCP can then propagate a constant across it.

This compounds with #1374, which is about four passes ignoring the barrier outright; here the barrier itself can be computed wrong.

**Cleanup:** replace the body of `tokenise_command_words` with a call to `segment_commands_with_offset_and_config(text, 0, config)` and map each `SegmentedCommand` to the four facts `dynamic_names` wants — `text` from `SegmentedCommand::texts`, `braced_literal` from `argv[i].kind == Str && single_token_word[i]`, `substituted` from the word's `WordExpr` (`ir.rs:437`, which already distinguishes `Variable` / `CommandSubstitution` / `Template`), and the raw spelling from the word span. Thread the document's `LexerConfig` into `dynamic_name_barrier` so the barrier is computed under the same dialect as the IR. ~40 lines deleted, one config parameter threaded.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: `tcl-compiler` lowering hand-rolls a var/param-list splitter (`parse_param_names`, 8 call sites) that mis-splits `a\ b` and `{a b}` — the analyser, `signature_scan`, and both runtimes use the shared list codec
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the cross-surface centralisation audit following #1419's numeral-parser precedent (sibling of the #1371/#1400 legacy-duplication audit). The lowering stage parses every `proc`/`foreach`/`lmap`/`dict for`/`array for`/`try on|trap` name list with a private byte scanner instead of the shared list/formal-parameter codec that every other consumer in the tree — including the analyser looking at the very same source word — already uses.

## The shared owner

`tcl_syntax::formal_params::parse_formal_parameters` is the declared owner of `proc`-style parameter lists: `split_list` of the outer list, then `split_list` of each specifier (`rust/tcl-syntax/src/formal_params.rs:111`). The VM (`rust/tcl-vm/src/command.rs:1148`), the WASM runtime (`runtime/rust/src/cmd_proc.rs:70`), and `tcl-compiler`'s own `signature_scan` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/signature_scan/params.rs:193`, with `spec_to_param` documenting `{a\ b}` → the single name `a b`) all route through it. The analyser's `define_vars_from_list` — which handles the identical `foreach` varList word the lowerer also reads — uses plain `tcl_syntax::list::split_list` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:3933`).

## The hand-rolled copy

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/lowering/mod.rs:303`'s `parse_param_names` instead does its own whitespace-skip-and-brace-count scan. A braced element is reduced to `inner.split_whitespace().next()` — one name, discarding the rest of a multi-word braced specifier (`mod.rs:334`) — and the bare-word arm stops at any space with no backslash awareness at all, so `a\ b` becomes two names (`mod.rs:341`). It is called at 8 sites: `foreach`/`lmap` var lists and `foreachLine` (`rust/tcl-compiler/src/lowering/structured.rs:445`, also 577/686/983), and `proc` params, apply-lambda, `array for`, and OO method params (`lowering/mod.rs:1474`, also 2109/2167/2806).

## Divergence

```tcl
foreach {{a b}} {1} {puts hi}
# tclsh, and the analyser's define_vars_from_list: one variable, literally named "a b"
# the lowerer: the single name "a" - binds the wrong variable

foreach {a\ b} {1} {}
# tclsh, and the analyser: one variable "a b"
# the lowerer: two variables "a\" and "b"

proc p {a\ b} {}
# tclsh, the VM, runtime/rust, and signature_scan: one required parameter "a b"
# the lowering stage: two parameters - wrong arity for the lowered Procedure
```

## Why it matters

The lowerer's variable bindings and parameter arity feed the compiled program directly, so a `foreach`/`proc` specifier with a braced multi-word name or a backslash-escaped space silently binds the wrong variable or reports the wrong arity — while the analyser, looking at the very same source, reports the correct name.

## Relationship to open issues

Adjacent to #1388 (collapsing four scope-alias parsers) and #1378 (switch clause-list hand-rolled in three analyser sites) in spirit only — those are `upvar`/`switch` sites in the analyser. This is the lowering stage's parameter/variable-list splitter, whose owner already exists and is already used by every other consumer in the tree, including `tcl-compiler`'s own `signature_scan`.

## Cleanup

Replace `parse_param_names` with the shared owner: `tcl_syntax::formal_params::parse_formal_parameters` for the *formal-parameter* sites (proc / apply / OO methods), and plain `tcl_syntax::list::split_list` for the *variable-list* sites (`foreach`, `lmap`, `foreachLine`, `dict for|map`, `array for`, `try on|trap`) — the two are different grammars and the current single helper conflates them. `signature_scan/params.rs` already demonstrates both shapes over `find_element`.

**Scale:** medium — 8 call sites across two lowering files, but a mechanical substitution with both target APIs already proven in the same crate.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Cross-file path constants: resolve a source path through a variable another document assigns
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Summary

Extend the path-constant tier (#775) across document boundaries: a computed `source` path reading a variable that a *different* file assigns should resolve when the source graph proves which assignment is in effect.

The per-document tier deliberately stops at the file edge. The #1181 corpus shows exactly one project paying for that: OSVVM-Scripts, where `StartUp.tcl` assigns `::osvvm::OsvvmScriptDirectory` once and ~12 sibling scripts do

```tcl
source ${::osvvm::OsvvmScriptDirectory}/OsvvmScriptsCore.tcl
```

Every one of those abstains today, while the assigning file's own sources fold. tcllib's `doctools` `$srcdir` shape is adjacent.

## Why this is a load-order question, not a lookup

Which value a reading document sees depends on *when it runs*: the variable exists only after the assigning document has executed, and the reader is (in the OSVVM shape) sourced *by* the assigner. "Take the value from wherever it is assigned" is exactly the guess the per-document fact was designed not to make — a workspace can hold two files assigning the same name, or a reader that runs before the writer.

The index already holds both halves of the answer:

- `WorkspaceIndex::path_constant_assignments(uri)` — every document's raw `PathConstantWrite` facts (top-level `set`s plus `variable`/`set` in literal `namespace eval` bodies, with `Raw`/`Declared`/`Poisoned` distinguished and each write's execution namespace recorded).
- `RunOrder` (`docs/design/contracts/workspace-indexing.md`) — the source + package load order, which already answers `None` for multi-site files and cycles.

## Required design

- A reading document's unresolved variable resolves from a **source-graph ancestor** that assigns it, only when the order proves the assignment runs before the read. `RunOrder`'s existing abstentions (incomparable, multi-site, cycle, no resolver) must fall through to abstention here too.
- **Workspace-wide single-writer poisoning**: a name assigned in more than one document is dropped outright unless the order makes exactly one assignment visible to the reader — the same last-write/first-write argument as the per-document poison, one level up.
- **Stratification, stated and proved**: cross-file constants consult the load order, and the edges the constants unlock feed the load order. Build the order from same-document-resolvable edges first, then resolve cross-file constants against it, then admit the newly resolvable edges; if iterated, the fixpoint must be monotone (edges are only ever added, never re-answered differently) and terminating. An edge must never resolve one way on the first pass and another way later in the same generation.
- **Invalidation**: a document's constant facts already sit in `SettlementDependencies`; cross-file resolution makes *other* documents' edges depend on them, so a constants change must refresh dependent documents' links/edges the way package facts already do.
- All existing consumers inherit the tier through the same shared evaluator (`auto_path_eval`) — document links, `resolve_source_edge`, load-order ranking, `auto_path` folding. No consumer grows private cross-file logic.

## Acceptance criteria

- OSVVM-Scripts' `${::osvvm::OsvvmScriptDirectory}/…` sources resolve (12 abstentions today), verified against the #1181 corpus checkout with the folded-target-exists oracle; **zero new folded-but-missing results** across the corpus.
- Tk's `$::ttk::library` still abstains — its assignment is if-guarded, so no order makes the value static; cross-file must not relax the guarded-write rule.
- A name assigned in two documents abstains unless the order disambiguates; a reader on a cycle or with two source sites abstains.
- Go-to-definition/references through a cross-file-constant `source` agree with the document link on the same line (e2e, both directions).
- Tests cover: the OSVVM shape, two-writer ambiguity, reader-before-writer order, cycle/multi-parent abstention, stratification (an edge unlocked by a cross-file constant does not re-rank an edge already resolved), and invalidation on constant change.
- The document-links KCS note and `workspace-indexing.md` contract updated in the same change.

## Non-goals

- Guarded writes (`if {[info exists …]}`), proc-body writes, `$env(...)`, `$argv`/`$argv0`, and the interpreter's runtime cwd — outside any static order's knowledge.
- Values crossing `package require` boundaries via `pkgIndex.tcl` machinery (`$dir` in `package ifneeded` scripts is the loader's contextual variable, not a workspace constant).
- Relaxing per-document poisoning rules in the name of coverage.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: The differential fuzzer covers only two backend pairs and folds every error to a bool, so eBPF, `runtime/rust`, the real linked WASM runtime, and all error-message text are never differentially validated
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
`rust/tcl-fuzz` runs two comparisons, and neither reaches three of the four execution backends.

**Pair 1** — `rust/tcl-fuzz/src/campaign.rs:100-101`:

```rust
let reference = run_backend(self.tclsh, &path, self.timeout);
let subject   = run_backend(self.tclvm, &path, self.timeout);
```

**Pair 2** — `rust/tcl-fuzz/src/wasm_diff.rs`, which its own module doc describes accurately: both sides evaluate leaf commands on `tcl-vm`, and the only variable is whether control flow comes from the WASM emitter or from `tcl-vm`. That isolates a WASM control-flow miscompile, which is genuinely useful, but it is a self-consistency check — no WASM *runtime* is involved.

Never compared:

- **eBPF against anything.** `rust/tcl-fuzz/Cargo.toml` has no `bpf-*` dependency and `grep -rniE 'bpf' rust/tcl-fuzz/src/` returns nothing.
- **`runtime/rust` against anything** — not against `tclsh`, not against `tcl-vm`. This is the backend that #1309 shows silently corrupting binary strings on the whole portable `string` surface; a `runtime/rust`-vs-`tclsh` arm would have caught it on the first seed that emitted `string index` over `binary format` output.
- **The real linked WASM runtime.** `wasm_diff` embeds `wasmtime` with a `tcl-vm`-backed host, so the emitted module is never linked against `runtime/rust`'s wasm32 build.
- **`tclsh` cross-version.** One oracle, one version.

## Error text is never compared

`rust/tcl-fuzz/src/harness.rs:114-142`:

```rust
if re != se {
    Verdict::StatusMismatch
} else if !re && rs != ss {
    Verdict::StdoutMismatch
} else {
    Verdict::Match
}
```

`errored` is a bool, and stdout is compared *only when neither side errored*. So two backends that both fail agree by construction, whatever they say — the entire `errorCode`/`errorInfo`/message surface is outside the differential. Given how much of the tcltest corpus asserts on message text, this is a large blind spot in the one arm that does have a real oracle.

## Suggested order

1. `runtime/rust` ↔ `tclsh` — highest value per unit of work; the runtime is the least-covered backend and has a live oracle.
2. Compare error message text when both sides error, behind a flag so existing findings do not all reclassify at once.
3. `tcl-vm` ↔ `runtime/rust` — no external oracle needed, catches backend drift directly.
4. Real linked WASM, and eBPF (which needs its own generator — the accepted surface is a small typed subset, see `rust-issues/RUST_ISSUE_145.md`).

Recorded until now only as `rust-issues/RUST_ISSUE_014.md`, which is one of the six entries still open in that sweep and has no GitHub issue. Re-verified against the branch tip.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: `runtime/rust`: case-changing `string` subcommands are a no-op on raw binary values, because one byte buffer serves both the string rep and the byte-array payload
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Split out of the residual limitation documented in [`docs/kcs/kcs-issue-runtime-string-subcommands-corrupt-binary-values.md`](../blob/rust/docs/kcs/kcs-issue-runtime-string-subcommands-corrupt-binary-values.md). The original corruption in that note (`ValueOps::as_str` replacing non-UTF-8 bytes with U+FFFD) was fixed under #1309 and that issue is closed; this is the part the fix deliberately left behind, and it had no issue of its own.

## Symptom

A case-changing `string` subcommand (`toupper` / `tolower` / `totitle`) applied to a value that *is* raw binary content is a no-op on the escaped bytes, instead of the byte-for-byte Latin-1 case fold C Tcl's byte-array shimmer performs.

```tcl
puts [binary encode hex [string toupper [binary format H* 41ff42]]]
```

| Backend | Result |
|---|---|
| `tclsh8.6` | `417842` |
| `tclsh9.0` | error: `expected code point values below 0xff but value at byte offset 1 was 0x178` |
| `tcl-vm` (`cargo run -p tcl-vm-cli`) | `417842` — matches 8.6 |
| `runtime/rust` (`cargo run --example run_script`) | **`41ff42`** — unchanged |

Note the 8.6/9.0 split: 0xFF upper-cases to U+0178, which 9.0 refuses to encode as a byte, so "correct" here is version-dependent and any fix has to pick per-version behaviour rather than a single answer. `tcl-vm` already agrees with 8.6.

## Root cause, as documented

`runtime/rust`'s `TclObj` has one byte buffer serving both roles real Tcl keeps separate: the object's string rep (what `puts` writes) and a byte-array's raw payload (what `binary encode`/`scan` read). Genuine non-ASCII text round-trips correctly through `bytes_to_str`/`str_to_bytes` (e.g. `string toupper "café"` → `"CAFÉ"`), but a value that is raw binary content is carried through the escape range, where the case fold does not apply.

The seam is `bytes_to_str` / `str_to_bytes` in `runtime/rust/src/value_ops.rs`; the trade-off is also referenced from `docs/design/runtime/c-extension-abi.md` §4.2.

## Scope

`runtime/rust` only. Not the bytecode VM (which is correct here), and this needs no change to the compiler or codegen.

Found while auditing the KCS corpus for documented gaps without tracking issues (PR #1346).

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Extract-into-proc refactor loses caller-frame writes and control-flow semantics
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Problem

`extract_proc_action` is offered for any non-empty line selection. It determines inputs with a textual `$var` scan, creates a top-level proc, and replaces the selection with a call. It performs no output-variable, frame, control-flow, namespace, or registry analysis.

Example, selecting the middle two statements:

```tcl
set x 0
set x 1
puts $x
puts "after=$x"
```

Original C Tcl 9.0.3 output:

```text
1
after=1
```

The generated shape is equivalent to:

```tcl
proc extracted_proc {x} {
    set x 1
    puts $x
}
set x 0
extracted_proc $x
puts "after=$x"
```

which prints `after=0`. The write moved into a private proc local.

Other unsound surfaces include `return`, `break`, `continue`, `yield`, `upvar`/global/variable, traces, arrays, dynamic names, namespace context, TclOO `my/self/next`, `info level/frame`, errors, and commands whose bodies/callbacks are registry-declared.

The refactor also inserts the new proc at line 0, potentially before namespace/package/dialect setup and with a colliding public name.

## Fix direction

Build extraction from CFG/SSA/place/effect analysis:

- compute live-ins and live-outs, including whole-array/member places and alias sets;
- preserve caller writes via an explicit result protocol or a registry-described `upvar` strategy;
- reject non-local control transfers and frame-sensitive effects unless a proven transform exists;
- place the definition in the correct namespace/interpreter/class context;
- choose a collision-free name using workspace symbols;
- preview grouped edits atomically.

Command/frame sensitivity must come from CommandRegistry traits/hooks, not a keyword list in the action.

## Tests and acceptance

- Execute original/refactored programs under C Tcl 9 and compare stdout, result/options, variables, traces, and errors.
- TP: pure selection with explicit live-ins and no live-outs.
- FP/TN/FN: scalar/array writes, read-modify-write, aliases, globals, return/break/continue, callbacks, TclOO, namespace eval, safe/sub-interpreters, and dynamic names.
- Add core refactor tests, native LSP e2e applying grouped edits, and VS Code selection/apply/undo tests.
- Document supported selections, refusal reasons, and examples.

Do not add clippy allows.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: W302 catch-result quick fixes insert after `catch`, not after its body
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Problem

The two W302 quick fixes produce a semantics-changing edit.

Input:

```tcl
set rc [catch {error oops} result]
puts [list $rc $result]
```

The intended result-capture form prints, under C Tcl 9.0.3:

```text
1 oops
```

For a bare `catch {error oops}`, W302 is anchored to `cmd_tok.span` — only the word `catch`. `code_actions` nevertheless treats the diagnostic end as if it were after the body's closing brace and inserts ` result` there. Applying the action creates:

```tcl
catch result {error oops}
```

C Tcl interprets `result` as the body and `error oops` as the result-variable name. The observable result is:

```text
1 {invalid command name "result"}
```

The `result opts` action is corrupted the same way.

Existing tests assert only the inserted text and that the range is zero-width; they do not assert the position or execute the result.

## Fix direction

Attach the complete insertion span to the diagnostic as a normal `CodeFix`, computed from the parsed invocation/argument token boundary. The code-action provider should only lift fixes; it should not reconstruct catch grammar from the diagnostic code.

The position must handle multiline bodies, trailing comments, semicolon-separated commands, leading `::catch`, aliases where statically proven, and malformed/incomplete source. Command shape belongs in the registry/lowering facts, not a `W302` branch in the LSP.

## Tests and acceptance

- Applying either action yields `catch BODY result` or `catch BODY result opts`.
- Execute before/after reproducers with C Tcl 9 and compare completion code, result, and options.
- TP/FP/TN/FN: one-line/multiline body, comments, semicolons, nested substitutions, existing result/options, malformed catch, qualified/static-alias calls, and dynamic heads.
- Add analyser fix-span tests, core edit-application tests, native LSP e2e tests, and VS Code tests which apply the WorkspaceEdit and inspect the document.
- Update W302 documentation with the exact transformed example and limits.

Do not add clippy allows.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: `existence_constant_branches` folds `info exists` on TclOO instance variables — false O100/I230 on both check paths
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found while fixing #1117 (the memo-path coverage gap): of the 20 hints the fix restores on `generalClasses.tcl`, **17 are false positives that affect the fresh path, the CLI, and the analyser's I230 identically today** — this is a separate, pre-existing defect in the shared helper, not a memoisation bug.

`sccp::existence_constant_branches` explicitly refuses to fold `info exists X` when `X` is a `global`/`variable`/`upvar`/`namespace upvar` scope alias, but is blind to **TclOO instance variables** — exactly such an implicit binding. So `if {[info exists Params]}` inside a method/destructor of a class declaring `variable name Params Pins` folds to a constant branch (O100) and fires I230, even though the variable's existence is genuinely dynamic per-instance state. Verified live: I230 fires on a method-body copy of code whose proc-body copy is clean.

Fix direction: treat a name in the enclosing class's variable list (and `my variable` declarations) as a scope alias in the existence-fold guard — abstain, as the helper already does for the other four binding forms. Needs instance-variable facts threaded into `FunctionUnit::build_full`; blast radius is I230, the O101 fold, and DCE, so it wants its own delta measurement over the OO corpus (the #1117 fixture files are ready-made: `generalClasses.tcl` should lose ~17 O100s and its method-body I230s).

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Settle the keyword / function / declaration taxonomy for Tcl highlighting
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## The question

Tcl has **no reserved words** — `if`, `puts` and `proc` are all just commands. "Is this a keyword?" is therefore a *colouring convention*, not a fact about the language, and we should follow the convention rather than invent one.

The trigger was a visible incoherence:

```tcl
catch { error boom } msg     ;# catch -> keyword.control.tcl
                             ;# error -> support.function.tcl
```

Two halves of one construct, two different colours.

## What the other grammars actually do

I fetched and read the real grammar files. **Two commonly-held assumptions turned out to be wrong:**

1. **VS Code ships no Tcl grammar.** There is no `extensions/tcl` — it 404s at every tag checked. The most-installed VS Code Tcl grammar is `rashwell.tcl` (197k installs), whose `tcl.tmLanguage` carries UUID `F01F22AC-7CBB-11D9-9B10-000A95E13C98` — **byte-identical to the 2005 TextMate bundle**.
2. **`support.function.tcl` appears in neither TextMate nor Sublime** (zero `support.*` hits in both). Their split is `keyword.control` vs `keyword.**other**` — they have *no function category at all*.

| source | control bucket | everything else |
|---|---|---|
| [TextMate `tcl.tmbundle`](https://github.com/textmate/tcl.tmbundle) | `if while for catch return break continue switch exit foreach` + `then elseif else` | `keyword.other.tcl` — one flat list of ~90 names incl. `error`, `puts`, `set`, `expr`, `lindex`. Scraped from the 8.4 command index, so it also contains man-page names (`SafeBase`, `tclvars`) — not a considered taxonomy. |
| [Sublime `TCL/Tcl.sublime-syntax`](https://github.com/sublimehq/Packages) | same list, verbatim | same list, artifacts and all. **But** adds proc params → `variable.parameter`, `namespace eval NAME` → `entity.name.namespace`, and **user commands → `variable.function`** |
| [tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-tcl](https://github.com/tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-tcl) | `@keyword.conditional` / `@keyword.repeat` | `@function.builtin` for `puts cd exec incr info join`; `@keyword` for a hand list that oddly includes `lindex list llength lsort` |
| [Pygments `TclLexer`](https://github.com/pygments/pygments/blob/master/pygments/lexers/tcl.py) | `Keyword`: incl. **`error`**, `eval`, `expr`, `proc`, `set`, `uplevel`, `upvar` | `Name.Builtin`: `puts lindex string dict clock exec …` |
| `go2sh.tcl-language-support` (the one independent VS Code grammar, also LSP-backed) | **only** `if else for foreach while break continue` | `entity.name.function` for every other command; **`proc` → `storage.type.function`**; `support.function.{namespace,expr,dict}` |
| [Zed `kissb-zed-tcl`](https://github.com/richnou/kissb-zed-tcl) | — | `@operator` for `break catch continue error return throw try`; `@function.builtin` for the rest |

### Consensus

- Every source uses a **two-bucket model**: a small control bucket + a large everything-else bucket. Names differ wildly; the *shape* is universal.
- **Hard-consensus control set**: `if else elseif while for foreach break continue` (+ `switch` in 5 of 6). That is all.
- **`proc` is never control flow** — always a distinct declaration-ish scope.
- **`puts` is never a keyword** in any grammar that *has* a function category. TextMate/Sublime lump it with keywords only because they have nowhere else to put it. That is a 2005 limitation, not a claim, and copying it would be over-reading.
- **`error` is never a plain function**: `keyword.other` (TextMate), `Keyword` (Pygments), `@keyword` (tree-sitter), `@operator` (Zed). Only go2sh — which special-cases almost nothing — leaves it generic.
- **Nobody scopes TclOO.** No `oo::`, `class`, `method`, `superclass`, `my`, `next`, `self` in any of the seven. Greenfield: no convention to follow, none to violate.

### Genuine disagreement

`expr` (Keyword vs `@function.builtin` vs `support.function` — a 3-way split), `catch`, and `exit` (`keyword.control` in TextMate vs `Name.Builtin` in Pygments — a flat contradiction).

## The synthesised taxonomy

Melding the survey above with a conventional-scope proposal. The governing rule:

> **A built-in that primarily computes → `support.function`. A built-in that changes evaluation or control flow → `keyword.control`.**

And the cross-layer invariant, which is what actually keeps this honest:

> **The grammar may be *less specific* than the semantic layer — never *differently coloured*.** It may emit `entity.name.type.bigip` where the server emits `entity.name.type.pool.bigip`; it may not emit `support.function` where the server emits `keyword`.

### Adopted — and already shipped in this PR

| construct | scope | evidence |
|---|---|---|
| `catch` `try` `throw` **`error`** | `keyword.control.tcl` | 4 of 5 category-aware grammars call `error` keyword-ish |
| `proc` `method` `constructor` | `storage.type.function.tcl` | go2sh does exactly this; Sublime's own naming guide recommends it |
| proc/method name | `entity.name.function.tcl` | universal across the TextMate lineage |
| parameters | `variable.parameter.tcl` | Sublime does exactly this |
| `oo::class create` / `oo::define` | `support.class.tcl` | greenfield |
| class name | `entity.name.class.tcl` | greenfield |
| `superclass` / `mixin` | `storage.modifier.tcl` | greenfield |
| `puts` `lindex` `string` `info` | `support.function.tcl` (unchanged) | every grammar with a function category |

`error` was fixed at the **registry** (`Traits::LANGUAGE_KEYWORD`), so one edit moved it in the semantic legend *and* all three generated TextMate-family grammars *and* the Zed queries at once.

### Rejected — with reason

**`my` / `self` / `next` → `variable.language.tcl` in the grammar.** These are *deliberately* excluded from every generated grammar (`CONTEXT_SENSITIVE_EXCLUDE` in `gen_tmlanguage_keywords.rs`): a context-free regex blanket-matching `my`, `next`, `self` false-positives constantly, because they are ordinary variable and proc names in non-TclOO code. The semantic layer already types them correctly — it knows whether it is inside a method body; a static grammar cannot. This is a lesson the codebase has already paid for, and the conventional-scope argument does not outweigh it. **Semantic-only.**

### Still open — deliberate follow-ups, not oversights

1. **User command invocation → `variable.function.tcl`.** Sublime does this and it is a real gap (we scope user commands as *nothing* today). Needs care: "a bareword in command position that is not a known builtin" is expressible in TextMate but false-positive-prone, so it wants its own change with tests.
2. **Sub-buckets** — `keyword.control.exception.tcl` (catch/try/throw/error), `.conditional` (if/then/elseif/else), `.import` (source). Cheap and prefix-safe (a theme targeting `keyword.control` still matches), but requires expanding the generator's 3-bucket model.
3. **Ensemble subcommands → `support.function.<ensemble>.tcl`** (`string length`, `dict get`).
4. **`eval` / `uplevel` / `upvar` → `keyword.control`.** I'd *push back* here: the evidence is genuinely mixed (TextMate has them in `keyword.other`, where they sit today), and they are scoping/declaration words more than control-flow words. Low value, non-trivial churn. Leaving them as keywords-but-not-control unless there's a reason.
5. **LSP modifiers**: `defaultLibrary` on built-ins, `property` for TclOO instance variables.
6. **Zed**: tree-sitter captures for class/method (`@type`, `@constructor`). Blocked on the upstream Tcl grammar having no TclOO nodes.

## Note

`error` changing colour (function → control keyword) is **user-visible** and belongs in the release notes.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Align the TextMate / Sublime / tree-sitter grammars with the semantic-token vocabulary
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Summary

v2.1.7 overhauled the **semantic** token layer: 57 types, zero overlapping pairs, BIG-IP configs and APL presentations first-class for the first time. The **grammar** layer — TextMate (VS Code), `.sublime-syntax`, tree-sitter (Zed) — did not move with it, and is now the lagging layer.

This matters because the grammar is not a redundant second opinion. It is:

- the paint you see **before** the server responds (and on files too large for semantic tokens),
- the **only** paint where the server never runs — GitHub/Linguist, a plain Sublime install, Zed without the extension.

Where the two layers disagree you get a visible colour flip on open, and a *wrong* static fallback everywhere the LSP is absent.

## What is already aligned — leave it alone

The command-classification split (**keyword vs function**) is already generated from `tcl-registry` for both the TextMate-family grammars (`xtask/src/gen_editor_catalogs.rs`) and the Zed queries (`xtask/src/gen_zed_queries.rs`), with a drift gate in `make`. `tcl.tmLanguage.json` carries exactly two generated alternation lists — `keyword.control.tcl` and `support.function.tcl` — and `highlights.scm` carries the same lists as `#any-of?` predicates behind a `DO NOT EDIT` header.

So `catch` is a `keyword` semantically **and** `keyword.control.tcl` in TextMate; `puts` is a `function` **and** `support.function.tcl`. That agrees today and stays agreeing by construction. Good.

The gaps are everything the grammar can't express *contextually*, plus two whole languages.

## Gap 1 — VS Code has no grammar for BIG-IP configs or APL

`package.json` contributes **one** grammar for all fifteen languages:

```
tcl-apl    -> ./syntaxes/tcl.tmLanguage.json
tcl-bigip  -> ./syntaxes/tcl.tmLanguage.json
```

That file contains **zero** BIG-IP patterns and **zero** APL patterns (no `partition`, `ltm rule`, `pool`, `monitor`, no APL `section`/`field`). A `bigip.conf` is therefore painted with *Tcl* rules — which is simply wrong — and is then wholly replaced by a 34-type BIG-IP token stream when the server answers. Same for APL (12 types).

The 22 new types (10 `apl*`, 12 BIG-IP) have no grammar counterpart in VS Code at all.

## Gap 2 — Zed ships no highlights for APL or TMSH

```
editors/zed/languages/apl/    config.toml (grammar = "tcl")   highlights.scm: MISSING
editors/zed/languages/tmsh/   config.toml (grammar = "tcl")   highlights.scm: MISSING
```

Both declare the Tcl grammar and neither ships a query file, so they get no highlighting pre-LSP.

## Gap 3 — Sublime has APL but no BIG-IP

`editors/sublime-text/` has a dedicated `APL.sublime-syntax` (good — VS Code should have its equivalent) but **no** BIG-IP config syntax.

## Gap 4 — the TclOO/parameter types paint nowhere, and the editors disagree with each other

v2.1.7 added `parameter`, `method` and `class`. In the grammar layer:

| | `variable.parameter` | class | method |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tcl.tmLanguage.json` | **0 hits** | **0 hits** (no `entity.name.class`, no `storage.type`) | none |
| Zed `tcl/highlights.scm` | **`@variable.parameter` present** | none | none |

So a proc's parameters highlight in Zed and *don't* in VS Code, on the same file, before the LSP lands — the two editors disagree with each other. And `class` / `method` are painted by nobody until the server answers.

These are all reachable with ordinary TextMate `begin`/`end` context rules (`proc NAME {params}`, `oo::class create NAME`, `method NAME {params}`), so "the grammar can't know" is not the obstacle here — nobody has written them.

## Open design question (affects all three layers at once)

`throw`, `return`, `break` and `continue` are `keyword`; **`error` is `function`** — although all five are non-local exits. Whichever way we settle it, the answer propagates automatically to TextMate, Sublime and Zed, because those lists are generated. Worth settling deliberately rather than by accident.

## Proposed

1. A real BIG-IP config grammar and a real APL grammar for VS Code (and a BIG-IP one for Sublime), instead of pointing both at the Tcl grammar.
2. `highlights.scm` for Zed's `apl/` and `tmsh/`.
3. Context rules for `parameter` / `class` / `method` in the TextMate grammar, so the pre-LSP paint agrees with the semantic paint instead of flipping — and so VS Code and Zed agree with each other.
4. Extend the generator to emit these too, wherever they're derivable from the registry, so they stay in sync like the keyword/function lists already do.
5. Settle `error` vs `throw`.

The target isn't grammar/semantic identity — a grammar can't resolve a `namespace import` alias, and shouldn't try. The target is **no contradiction**: the grammar may be less specific than the semantic layer, but it must never paint a span a *different* colour than the server is about to.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: Semantic tokens: correctness audit and target state (1.11.4 ↔ 2.1.6 differential)
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
A differential audit of `textDocument/semanticTokens/full` between **v1.11.4** (Python server) and **v2.1.6** (native Rust server), to establish the **target state** for semantic tokens. **This is not a "restore 1.11.4" ticket.** 2.1.6 made real architectural advances that must be preserved, and 1.11.4 was wrong — sometimes invalidly so — in several of the places where it looks richer. For each item below the target is stated explicitly, and in **five cases the target is neither server's current behaviour** (§1, §2, §3, §9, §10).
Method Both servers driven over raw JSON-RPC with **identical file bytes**, one fresh server per file, decoding each server's tokens with its own `initialize` legend. Three corpora: - **A — repo samples**: 16 Tcl/iRule files from `samples/`. 1.11.4: 3,183 tokens; 2.1.6: 3,278. - **B — real-world Tcl, ~30k lines / 28 files**: Tcl 8.6.16 and 9.0.3 core library (`init`, `clock`, `safe`, `package`, `history`, `word`, `tm`, `auto` from each), plus TclOO-heavy libraries — [ruff](https://github.com/nico-robert/ruff), [zesty](https://github.com/nico-robert/zesty), [ticklecharts](https://github.com/nico-robert/ticklecharts), [tomato](https://github.com/nico-robert/tomato). 1.11.4: 66,107 tokens; 2.1.6: 67,446; 59,555 spans identical. - **C — dialects**: `samples/bigip/bigip.conf`, `samples/bigip/bigip_base.conf`, `samples/apl/example.apl`. Counts are from corpus B unless stated. Notation: `'text':type[modifiers]`. Neither server errored on corpus B.
--- # Part 0 — What 2.1.6 got right (do not regress these) ### Zero overlapping tokens (1.11.4: 184) The LSP spec requires semantic tokens **not to overlap**. 1.11.4 violates this by layering a specific token on top of a generic one covering the same span; 2.1.6 emits none. | corpus | 1.11.4 overlapping pairs | 2.1.6 | |---|---|---| | A — samples | 5 | **0** | | B — real-world Tcl (30k lines) | 4 | **0** | | C — `example.apl` | **110** | **0** | | C — `bigip_base.conf` | **65** | **0** | Examples from 1.11.4: ``` bigip_base.conf:6 'Common':string OVERLAPS 'Common':partition example.apl:9 'define':function OVERLAPS 'define':aplDefine ``` **This is the single most important finding for §9 and §10.** 1.11.4's BIG-IP and APL highlighting was implemented by overlaying a second token on an existing one — the overlaps are concentrated almost entirely in exactly the two features 2.1.6 dropped. Reinstating those features means **reimplementing them non-overlapping**, not restoring the old code path. ### A leaner, more standard legend (53 → 32 types) 2.1.6 removed 21 bespoke types and added two standard ones. Against the LSP standard type list: - **2.1.6 standard**: `keyword, function, variable, string, number, comment, namespace, regexp, event, operator, decorator, enumMember, property` - **2.1.6 custom** (justified — no standard equivalent): `regexp*` ×7, `format*` ×4, `clock*` ×3, `binary*` ×3, `object`, `escape` - **1.11.4 misused a standard type**: it had `interface` in its legend — used for *BIG-IP network interfaces*, not the LSP meaning. Do not reinstate it that way. ### Genuine correctness fixes in 2.1.6 | case | 1.11.4 | 2.1.6 | |---|---|---| | empty string `""` | `'"':string` (1 char) ❌ | `'""':string` ✅ | | POSIX class `[[:digit:]]` | `'[[:digit:]':regexpCharClass` + `']':regexp` ❌ | `'[[:digit:]]':regexpCharClass` ✅ | | `variable name sides` in a class body | `'sides':string` ❌ | `'sides':variable[declaration]` ✅ | | `bigip.conf` | **crashes** — `-32603 IndexError` (`compiler/parsing/lexer.py:1157`) ❌ | no crash ✅ | | TclOO `my` / `next` / `self` | — | `keyword` ✅ | Plus ~1,150 of 1.11.4's `string` fallbacks resolved into real types (487 → `variable`, 252 → `decorator`, 236 → `namespace`, 97 → `keyword`, 54 → `property`, 28 → `enumMember` — e.g. iRule `priority`, previously a flat `string`), 225 functions gained `defaultLibrary`, and comments are now covered by semantic tokens rather than left to TextMate. --- # Part 1 — Target-state principles 1. **Standard LSP token types first.** Use a custom type only where no standard type fits. Never repurpose a standard type for an unrelated concept (see `interface`, above). 2. **Never emit overlapping tokens.** 2.1.6 achieves this; any reinstated feature must preserve it. 3. **Cover the full lexical extent of a token, with one consistent delimiter rule** across `"..."`, `{...}` and `${...}`. 4. **A generic-but-correct type beats a specific-but-wrong one — and both beat a whole-line `string` dump.** Falling back to "emit the entire line as one `string` token" (§9, and the iRule note in §12) is worse than emitting nothing, because it actively mis-colours code. --- # Part 2 — Findings ## 1. Literal words are truncated by one character — target is neither server The closing delimiter is never covered in 2.1.6, while the opener *is* — so literals are highlighted asymmetrically. But 1.11.4 was **also** inconsistent: it covered both quotes of a string, yet neither brace of a braced word. ```tcl set greeting "hello world" set braced {a b} set empty "" set bound 3 puts ${bound} puts [expr {${bound} + 1}] ``` | source | 1.11.4 | 2.1.6 | **target** | |---|---|---|---| | `"hello world"` | `'"hello world"':string` | `'"hello world':string` ❌ | `'"hello world"':string` | | `{a b}` | `'a b':string` (content only) ⚠️ | `'{a b':string` ❌ | `'{a b}':string` | | `""` | `'"':string` ❌ | `'""':string` ✅ | `'""':string` | | `${bound}` (arg) | `'${bound}':variable` | `'${bound':variable` ❌ | `'${bound}':variable` | | `${bound}` (in `expr`) | `'${bound}':variable` | `'${bound}':variable` ✅ | `'${bound}':variable` | Unaffected in 2.1.6, and a useful localisation: interpolated strings (`"$a and $b"` — the closing `"` is emitted as its own fragment) and `${var}` inside an `expr` body. **Likely cause.** `push_token` (`rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/semantic_tokens.rs:4942`) emits `span.start()..span.end()`, but the lexer's span convention — documented in the same file at `semantic_tokens.rs:3374` — is that **`span.end()` sits *at* the closing `}` / `"`**, with `content_offset` stripping the opener: > rebuild each element into a `Token` following the lexer's inner-end + `content_offset` convention (`span.end()` sits at the closing `}`/`"`; `content_offset` strips the opener) So `end - start` covers `opener + content` but excludes the terminator. Extend `end` by one for a delimited word whose terminator is present — without double-counting the empty-content clamp branch immediately above, and without touching the interpolated path where the closing `"` is already its own fragment. Regression test should pin all three shapes plus the two correct cases: `"str"`, `{braced}`, `${var}`, `""`, `expr {${var}}`. --- ## 2. TclOO — target is neither server; use the standard `method` and `class` types **245 occurrences.** The highest-impact item for object-oriented Tcl. 1.11.4's `function` was *better than 2.1.6's `string`, but still not right*: LSP has dedicated `method` and `class` types, and **neither server's legend contains either**. ```tcl oo::class create Shape { constructor {n s} { set name $n } method area {} { return 0 } method describe {{prefix "Shape:"}} { return "$prefix $name" } } oo::define Shape { method extra {} { return 1 } } ``` | source | 1.11.4 | 2.1.6 | **target** | |---|---|---|---| | `oo::class create Shape` — class name | `'Shape':string` ⚠️ | `'Shape':string` ⚠️ | `'Shape':class[definition]` | | `oo::define Shape` — class ref | `'Shape':string` ⚠️ | `'Shape':string` ⚠️ | `'Shape':class` | | `method area {}` | `'area':function[definition]` | `'area':string` ❌ | `'area':method[definition]` | | `method describe {…}` | `'describe':function[definition]` | `'describe':string` ❌ | `'describe':method[definition]` | | `method extra {}` (in `oo::define`) | `'extra':function[definition]` | `'extra':string` ❌ | `'extra':method[definition]` | | `constructor {n s}` — params | `'n':parameter[declaration]` | `'n':variable[declaration]` ❌ | `'n':parameter[declaration]` (see §4) | Note the class name is `string` in **both** servers — reinstating 1.11.4's behaviour would not fix it. **The machinery already exists in 2.1.6.** It resolves a method *call* correctly but not the *declaration*: ```tcl oo::class create C { method a {} { my b; next } # 2.1.6: 'my':keyword 'b':function ✅ (target: 'b':method) method b {} { return [self] } # 2.1.6: 'method':keyword 'b':string ❌ (target: 'b':method[definition]) } ``` So 2.1.6 knows `b` is a method when called via `my`, but types its declaration as a plain string. The declaration path simply isn't classifying the name word. `method`/`constructor`/`destructor`/`my`/`next`/`self` all resolve as keywords correctly. Distribution: `ruff/src/formatter.tcl` 56, `ticklecharts/chart.tcl` 49, `zesty/progressbar.tcl` 47, `ruff/src/formatter_html.tcl` 32, `zesty/table.tcl` 31, `tomato/Point3d.tcl` 20. --- ## 3. Array refs with a substituted index — target is neither server **250 occurrences.** A *literal* index is fine in both; a *substituted or computed* index makes 2.1.6 fall back to `string`. But 1.11.4's shape was also poor: it folded the `(` into the variable token and emitted the bare `)` as a second `variable[declaration]`. ```tcl set env(PATH) /usr/bin ;# literal index — identical in both ✅ set env($lo) $x unset UnknownPending($name) incr counts($k) ``` | source | 1.11.4 | 2.1.6 | **target** | |---|---|---|---| | `set env($lo) $x` | `'env(':variable[declaration]` `'$lo':variable` `')':variable[declaration]` ⚠️ | `'env(':string` `'$lo':variable` `')':string` ❌ | `'env':variable[declaration]` `'$lo':variable` — parens not part of the variable token | | `unset UnknownPending($name)` | `'UnknownPending(':variable[declaration]` … `')':variable[declaration]` ⚠️ | `'UnknownPending(':string` … `')':string` ❌ | `'UnknownPending':variable[declaration]` `'$name':variable` | Pervasive in the Tcl core library itself: `set env($lo)`, `set env([string toupper $lo])`, `unset UnknownPending($name)`, `set auto_index($name)`, `trace add variable env($p) write`. Distribution: `init.tcl` 76, `package.tcl` 68, `clock.tcl` 32, `ruff.tcl` 22, `history.tcl` 20, `safe.tcl` 12. --- ## 4. Restore the standard `parameter` type — 979 occurrences 2.1.6's legend has no `parameter`, so every proc / method / constructor argument emits as an ordinary `variable`, indistinguishable from a local. | source | 1.11.4 | 2.1.6 | **target** | |---|---|---|---| | `proc ::safe::Log {args} {}` | `'args':parameter[declaration]` | `'args':variable[declaration]` ❌ | `'args':parameter[declaration]` | | `constructor {n s} {` | `'n':parameter[declaration]` | `'n':variable[declaration]` ❌ | `'n':parameter[declaration]` | `parameter` is a standard LSP type and its removal is a plain loss of fidelity for every Tcl file. (If it was dropped deliberately, worth saying so and closing this item.) Note the *other* standard type 2.1.6 dropped, `interface`, should **not** come back — 1.11.4 was misusing it for BIG-IP interfaces (Part 0). --- ## 5. Regex: closing `)` of a group is typed `regexpQuantifier` — 148 occurrences ```tcl regexp {^(foo|bar)+([[:digit:]]+)$} $str -> a b ``` | token | 1.11.4 | 2.1.6 | **target** | |---|---|---|---| | `(` | `regexpGroup` | `regexpGroup` ✅ | `regexpGroup` | | `)` | `regexpGroup` | `regexpQuantifier` ❌ | `regexpGroup` | | `+` | `regexpQuantifier` | `regexpQuantifier` ✅ | `regexpQuantifier` | | `[[:digit:]]` | `'[[:digit:]':regexpCharClass` + `']':regexp` ❌ | `'[[:digit:]]':regexpCharClass` ✅ | `'[[:digit:]]':regexpCharClass` | Only the closer is misclassified — and the same expression shows 2.1.6 **fixing** 1.11.4's character-class truncation. Fix the `)` without regressing the class. --- ## 6. `expr`: parenthesis and ternary operator tokens are no longer emitted ```tcl set r [expr {($a + $b) * $c}] set t [expr {$a > 1 ? "yes" : "no"}] ``` | source | 1.11.4 | 2.1.6 | **target** | |---|---|---|---| | `($a + $b) * $c` | `'(':operator` `'+':operator` `')':operator` `'*':operator` | `'+':operator` `'*':operator` — parens gone ❌ | parens as `operator` | | `$a > 1 ? "yes" : "no"` | `'>':operator` `'?':operator` `':':operator` | `'>':operator` — `?` and `:` gone ❌ | `?` / `:` as `operator` | Arithmetic and comparison operators (`+`, `*`, `>`) still emit. uncatalogued_candidates.title: O103's argument-sensitive re-run folds a call to the final `return` past a `return` inside a `switch` arm the CFG keeps whole (miscompile)
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Repros

`tcl opt --profile full` versus tclsh 8.4.20 through 9.1.0 (all releases agree):

| program | `tcl opt` | tclsh |
|---|---|---|
| `proc p {x} {switch -glob -- $x {* {return 1}}; return 2}; puts [p abc]` | `puts 2` | `1` |
| `proc p {} {switch -glob -- [clock seconds] {* {return 1}}; return 2}; puts [p]` | `puts 2` | `1` |

The first program's body is itself rewritten to `return 1; return 2` by the switch fold, and the call still folds to the second return.

## Where

`resolve_return_constant` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/propagation.rs` reads only the CFG's `Return` terminators and fall-through exits, so a `return` inside a statement the CFG keeps whole (an opaque `switch` arm or default, a body the lowering does not split) is invisible to the re-run, which then folds the call to the later return. The syntactic summary does see the arm's `return`, which is why only the re-run folds these today. The reading must decline when an executable block holds a statement whose nested scripts can run a `return`: opaque `switch` arms, `if`/`for`/`while`/`foreach`/`try` bodies and handlers, a `Block`, an `UpFrame`; a `catch` body absorbs the return and is not descended.

Found while preparing value-transfer slice 7a on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42`, whose shared return reading would otherwise carry the miss into the summary too; fixed there in its own commit ahead of the slice.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: O109 deletes a store whose only read is a nested `[incr n]`, changing the program's output
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found while running the value-transfer worked examples through the CLI (`rust` at f02f327).

```tcl
set n 1
set result [incr n]
puts $result
puts $n
```

`tclsh9.0` prints `2` then `2`. `tcl opt FILE --profile full` reports `O109 Eliminate dead store` on `set n 1` and emits

```tcl
set result [incr n]
puts $result
puts $n
```

which prints `1` then `1` (Tcl 8.5+ creates an absent variable on `incr`; Tcl 8.4 raises `can't read "n"`).

**Cause.** The read-modify-write read that `incr` performs is only surfaced for a statement-level `Statement::Incr` (`collect_rmw_hidden_reads` in `rust/tcl-compiler/src/optimiser/elimination.rs`). An `incr` nested in a command substitution lowers as an ordinary call, its read of `n` is not a use in the def-use chains, and the preceding store looks dead.

**Expected.** No O109 and no W220: the store is read by the nested `incr`.

The value-transfer proposal on `claude/spectcl-optimization-discussion-5qhf42` (`docs/design/compiler/value-transfers.md`) makes a cell update's read an SSA use by construction; this program is one of its fixed witnesses.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: server: didOpen can wedge while holding the document map at db_source_matches
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
## Summary

The `v2.2.2` tag workflow's desktop VS Code extension suite wedged the native language server during `didOpen`. The server held the open-document map while suspended at `did_open: db_source_matches`; the document-sync barrier stopped advancing and unrelated requests then timed out.

This caused 8 integration-test failures. The failure appears intermittent: the immediately preceding `rust` CI run passed `test-ext`, and the release merge changed only `RELEASE_NOTES.md` relative to that passing commit.

## Occurrence

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Release | `v2.2.2` |
| Commit | `06a5e3451f1bf0ad2d91c5a258950037468658dc` |
| Workflow | [Release workflow run 33912351627](https://github.com/bitwisecook/tcl-lsp/actions/runs/33912351627) |
| Failed job | [test-ext job 101152805692](https://github.com/bitwisecook/tcl-lsp/actions/runs/33912351627/job/101152805692) |
| Result | 8 tests failed after the server stopped servicing requests |

## Decisive telemetry

The first timeout occurred while opening `indirectArray.tcl`. The liveness dump reported:

```text
VSCODE-WAIT-TIMEOUT waiting didOpen flush for indirectArray.tcl
LIVENESS: SERVER WEDGED
document-sync barrier has not advanced for 10s: now_serving=347, waiting for 348
turn held by didOpen on indirectArray.tcl, ticket 347
suspended at did_open: db_source_matches for 10.0s
open-document map held by did_open for 10.3s
```

The same holder telemetry repeated through the remaining failures. Additional observations:

- A document-free `getEffectiveConfig` request received no response for about 4 seconds.
- Hover on another document also received no response.
- The extension-host timer continued to fire normally, so the extension host itself was responsive.
- The server process remained alive (`S` state) with zero CPU-tick progress.
- Input bytes continued moving, but the server produced no output.
- Five server threads were waiting on futexes and one was reading fd 0, indicating the transport input path was still alive.
- No Salsa snapshot was reported outstanding.
- Waiters included `capture_job`, `publish_diagnostics_result`, and `deliver_fast_tier_if_current`; they could not advance because ticket 347 never released the turn/document-map holder.

## Blast radius

The stalled holder caused failures in these integration-test areas:

- Both indirect-array idiom cases
- `showReferences` setup
- SpecTcl torture setup
- SslicTcl authoring setup
- Two Variable Completion context-hook cases
- Workspace Symbols setup

The job ended with `Error: 8 test(s) failed`.

## Intermittency / comparison

The immediately preceding `rust` workflow passed the same desktop extension suite:

- Passing run: [33906717181](https://github.com/bitwisecook/tcl-lsp/actions/runs/33906717181)
- Passing `test-ext` job: [101134699935](https://github.com/bitwisecook/tcl-lsp/actions/runs/33906717181/job/101134699935)
- Commit: `17edcccbb` (parent of the release-notes merge)
- Duration: approximately 6m31s

The `v2.2.2` merge commit differs from that parent only in `RELEASE_NOTES.md`, so the server code under test is unchanged. That makes this look like a latent concurrency/liveness bug rather than a release-notes regression.

## Relationship to existing issues

- #1657 covered the earlier whole-server wedge after pack churn and was closed after containment. This occurrence is a concrete recurrence at the more precise `did_open: db_source_matches` suspension point.
- #1800 fixed a different holder path in `reindex_index_from_disk`; the holder here is `did_open`.
- #1678 remains open for diagnostics publishing holding the document map for a long time. It is related by lock/map contention, but the observed holder and suspension point here are different.

## Investigation points

- Why can `did_open` retain the open-document map and EditOrder ticket while awaiting `db_source_matches`?
- Can the awaited future/task become stuck, lose a notification, or be dropped without releasing the holder?
- Can `db_source_matches` or other potentially suspending work be moved outside the document-map critical section?
- Add focused watchdog/timeout telemetry around this await so a recurrence identifies the exact dependency being waited on.
- Ensure every cancellation/error path releases both the document map and EditOrder ticket.
- Add a deterministic concurrency regression test if the relevant ordering can be forced.

## Release handling

The failed tag job will be retried once the workflow attempt reaches a terminal state. A clean retry supports treating this as intermittent for `v2.2.2`; a repeat occurrence should block marketplace publication pending a fix.

uncatalogued_candidates.title: FunctionAnalysis and ModuleAnalysis are only ever default-constructed in their own tests
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found during a documentation audit, while checking a doc claim that `FunctionAnalysis` is "produced by `analyse_function()`". There is no `analyse_function` anywhere in the workspace.

## What is there

`rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyses.rs:175` declares `pub struct FunctionAnalysis`, and `:202`/`:204` declare a `ModuleAnalysis` holding `top_level: FunctionAnalysis` plus a `procedures` map. Every occurrence in the whole workspace is:

- the three declarations above,
- `FunctionAnalysis::default()` at `:256`, `:265`, and `:266` — all inside the module's own `#[cfg(test)]`,
- one mention in the crate-level doc comment, `rust/tcl-compiler/src/lib.rs:59`.

No production code constructs, returns, stores, or reads either type.

## The live path

The type that actually carries per-function analysis results is `FunctionUnit` in `compilation_unit.rs`, holding `cfg`, `ssa`, `def_use`, `sccp`, `types`, `taints`, `rendered_props`, `memory_ssa`, and the rest, built by `CompilationUnit::build_for()`. SCCP results come from `sccp()` returning `SccpResult`.

## Why it is not purely cosmetic

`FunctionAnalysis` is `pub` and named in the crate's top-level documentation, so it reads as part of the public API. **Eight documents** describe it as a pipeline data structure, and four of them attribute `FunctionUnit`'s fields to it (`def_use_chains`, `memory_ssa`, `rendered_props`): `docs/GLOSSARY.md`, `docs/design/compiler-architecture.md`, `docs/design/example-script-walkthroughs.md`, and `docs/design/compiler/{data-structure-reference,sccp-core-analyses,cfg-ssa-fact-model,dataflow-graph,rendered-value-properties}.md`.

The audit marked the two most prominent as "not on the live path" and pointed them here rather than deleting them, because nobody could tell whether the type is dead or merely not yet wired.

## Ask

Confirm it is dead and remove it (plus its `ModuleAnalysis` wrapper, the `lib.rs` mention, and the doc blocks), or say what it is for. Either answer unblocks the docs.

---

## Other names documented but absent from the tree

All verified with a whole-tree grep returning zero hits.

### `RuleInitExport`, `RuleInitVarDef`, `extract_rule_init_vars`

Described in `docs/design/compiler/event-priority-model.md`. Nothing carries a `base_priority` for cross-file `RULE_INIT` variable tracking. What exists is `Procedure::base_priority` per handler, and `static::` vars from `when RULE_INIT` tracked **per document** by `build_connection_scope()` (`connection_scope.rs`), whose `racy_static_defs` is the RULE_INIT-aware half and never spans files. So the documented cross-file capability is not merely unnamed — it is absent.

### `TokenRegion`, `NodeKind`, and three functions in `green-token-tree.md`

`TokenRegion` and `NodeKind` do not exist; nor do `infer_edit_range`, `incremental_top_level_chunks`, or `segment_top_level_chunks`. The real green layer is `GreenNode` + `SyntaxKind` in `parsing/syntax/green.rs`, and `SyntaxKind` has only `Document`/`Word`/`Command` — no error variant, so the `NodeKind::ERROR` tagging the doc describes has no counterpart.

**The document also contradicts the code outright**: `green.rs` states the green layer *"does not pointer-share subtrees, so there is no cross-edit reuse"*, which is the opposite of the memoised-descent and cross-consumer-sharing design sketched in its §§A–B. Sections A, B, and E are now marked as proposal; **§§C–D are equally forward-looking and are not yet marked**, and §D describes its property test as *"Shipped"*. Someone who knows the intent should decide whether this document is an unbuilt proposal or a stale description, and it should then be marked or corrected wholesale rather than section by section.

### `ProcLocalSummary` — this one asserts something false

`docs/design/example-script-walkthroughs.md` Example 24 traces a `ProcLocalSummary(...)` value. No such type exists. The phase-1 scan's real record is the private `LocalFacts` (`interprocedural.rs:1187`), whose fields differ substantially — no `qualified_name`, `params`, `arity`, `returns_constant`, `constant_return`, `return_depends_on_params`, or `return_passthrough_param`.

Worse, the traced value is wrong twice over: it shows `local_effect_writes=EffectRegion.LOG_IO`, but `EffectRegion` has no `LOG_IO` constant (only `NONE`, `HTTP_STATE`, `RESPONSE_LIFECYCLE`, `GLOBAL_STATE`, `UNKNOWN_STATE`), and `interprocedural.rs:716` resolves `puts`/`log` to `EffectRegion::NONE`. The trace was left in place rather than renamed, because any conversion would have had to change what it asserts.

### `VirtualToken`

Does not exist. The recovery mechanism it describes is real — `segment_with_recovery()` keeps a `ghosts: BTreeMap<u32, u8>` mapping source offset to inserted byte (`segmenter.rs:730`) — so the walkthrough trace was converted to that. But `VirtualToken` still appears as a term in `docs/GLOSSARY.md` and in `green-token-tree.md` §E.

### `CommandSpec::resolve_form`

Documented; no such method. Form resolution is `pick_form`.

`example-script-walkthroughs.md` traces `set x 42` as producing `LatticeValue(CONST, "42")` — a **string**. `parse_literal_value` (`sccp.rs:1906`) produces `ConstValue::Int(42)`, and there is an explicit test `parse_literal_value_prefers_int`. uncatalogued_candidates.title: Dead and unwired optimiser machinery: an unreachable second purity oracle in gvn.rs, and a `cross_event_vars` safety gate that is never populated
uncatalogued_candidates.body:
Found by the legacy-duplication audit following #1371. Two pieces of optimiser code document capabilities the shipped pipeline does not have. Both mislead a reader into believing a protection or an analysis is active.

---

## 1. Interprocedural purity reaches elimination but never GVN, and `gvn.rs` keeps an unwired duplicate of it

**The live fact:** `InterproceduralAnalysis::procedures[q].pure` (`interprocedural.rs:168`), computed by the `fixpoint_pure` least fixpoint over local purity ∧ callee purity (`:1040-1064`, driven from `:578-626`). Load-bearing: `elimination.rs:234-249` (`pure_call_targets`) projects it into the `PurityCtx` gating O109/O126/O108 RHS deletion (`:126-139`).

**The dead duplicate:** `gvn.rs` ships a parallel intra-module purity fixpoint — `PureProcs` (`:384`), `find_pure_procs` (`:437-460`), `function_body_is_pure` / `statement_is_pure` (`:464-531`), `is_pure_with_procs` (`:559`), `is_worth_reporting_with_procs` (`:573-592`) — the last documented as "user procs proved pure by intra-module analysis count as CSE candidates even if they don't carry the `CSE_CANDIDATE` registry trait".

A workspace-wide grep finds **zero production callers** of any of the five; only `gvn.rs`'s own `#[cfg(test)]` block (`:3306-3473`). Production GVN calls the registry-only `is_worth_reporting` (`:668-673`, used at `:1043` and `:1079`), and the modern semantic path requires `Traits::PURE | Traits::CSE_CANDIDATE` from the registry (`:896-900`) — which a user-defined proc can never carry.

**Consequence — a missed optimisation on the most valuable CSE shape in real Tcl:**

```tcl
proc double {a} { return [expr {$a * 2}] }
proc f {x} { set p [double $x]; set q [double $x]; return [list $p $q] }
```

`tcl explore --json` reports `interprocedural[0] = {"name": "::double", "pure": true, …}` and `gvn: []`. The compiler has *proved* the call reusable and no redundancy pass can see it — while `elimination` in the same run happily uses that same `pure` bit.

Secondary cost: ~130 lines of never-executed purity logic a reader will assume is live, whose judgement differs from `interprocedural`'s (e.g. `statement_is_pure` `:501-505` treats any unqualified `def` as proc-local-and-therefore-pure, a rule the interprocedural summary does not have).

**Cleanup:** decide which oracle wins and delete the other. Straightforward version: delete the five `gvn.rs` items and give `GvnSemanticFacts::from_function` (`:763`) access to the interprocedural summary, so an `InvocationResolution::Unresolved` head whose qualified name is in `interproc.procedures` with `pure: true` and no world barrier becomes `GvnSiteEligibility::Eligible` keyed on the qualified name. That is the larger half — the sidecar deliberately fails closed on unresolved names, so the summary needs projecting into `InvocationFacts`-shaped evidence rather than consulted as a name set. Alternatively a pure deletion if the capability is not wanted.

---

## 2. `PassContext::cross_event_vars` is written only inside `elimination::run`

**How it is derived:** inside `elimination::run`, from real analyses — `cu.connection_scope.cross_event_defs ∪ cross_event_imports` for `::when::*` procs (`elimination.rs:296-313`) and `ir_module.methods[q].instance_vars` for method bodies (`:333-340`). Stashed into `ctx.cross_event_vars`, consumed at `:551`, then restored (`:307`, `:324`, `:333`, `:357`).

**The problem:** `PassContext::cross_event_vars` (`optimiser/mod.rs:254`) is documented as shared state — "names whose values must be preserved across `when <event>` boundaries" — and is read as a safety gate by four other passes: `code_sinking.rs:79` (O125), `pattern_recognition.rs:142` (O119), `chain_fold.rs:74` (O104/O130), `propagation.rs:680` (O127).

The one production context builder, `manager::build_pass_context` (`manager.rs:132-144`), **never populates it**, and `elimination` `mem::take`s and restores it — so it is `HashSet::new()` for every one of those four readers. The `#[cfg(test)]` comment at `optimiser/mod.rs:526` ("cross_event_vars and next_group are intentionally preserved across functions") reads as if some caller fills it. None does.

**Largest exposure — O125 in an iRule:**

```tcl
when HTTP_REQUEST {
    if { [HTTP::header exists X] } { set n 1 } else { set n 2 }
    set flag $n
    if { $n > 1 } { log local0. "req $flag" }
}
when HTTP_RESPONSE { log local0. "resp $flag" }
```

`tcl opt --dialect f5-irules` emits O125 to sink `set flag $n` into the conditional branch even though `flag` is read in `HTTP_RESPONSE`.

Today the paired delete is dropped by `manager.rs:238 drop_def_elims_resurrected_by_replacements` (the insert text always re-mentions `$var`), so applying the surviving edit only duplicates the assignment rather than losing it — **the guard is currently latent rather than actively wrong**. That accident is exactly why it is worth fixing now: any refinement to the FP-OPT-08 guard turns this into "variable unset on the not-taken path" in a production iRule.

**Cleanup:** populate `cross_event_vars` once in `manager::build_pass_context` from `cu.connection_scope` (and per-function from `ir_module.methods[..].instance_vars` where the pass walks methods), and drop `elimination`'s local save/restore in favour of the shared value. If the per-function scoping `elimination` needs cannot be hoisted, replace the shared `PassContext` field with an explicit `fn cross_event_vars(cu, qname)` helper each pass calls — so a reader cannot mistake an empty default for "nothing is cross-event".

No user-visible change today (the guard only ever suppresses); after the FP-OPT-08 interaction is fixed it would suppress some O125 in iRules.
